column121: What happened: Aircraft Y was given a take off clearance for a runway that was occupied by a helicopter that had landed on the opposite end and was awaiting taxi instructions.What led to this:  The helicopter was coming in from the east and requested to land on the western side of the airport.  The active runways at the time were south to north (XXL and XXR).  The Tower cleared the helicopter to land on the numbers of an inactive runway XY; which would keep the helicopter on the eastern side of the airport; away from the flow of fixed wing traffic. About 5 minutes elapsed between the time the helicopter landed and Aircraft Y flew over the helicopter.During that time I believe the Controller may have been distracted by pattern traffic; Aircraft Z arrival (this was a factor prior to the helicopter landing which resulted in the controller deciding to keep the helicopter on the eastern side of the airport); a change in Aircraft Y IFR clearance; and by a pilot of an airplane who mistakenly made a final approach to the wrong parallel runway.Starting from the point at which the helicopter lands; the following exchanges were heard.Aircraft A was cleared for touch and go #2 behind Aircraft Z for runway XXL.Aircraft B was cleared to Land runway XXR.A few seconds after Aircraft B acknowledged the landing clearance the tower issue a taxi instruction to the airborne Aircraft B 'hold short of runway XXR I am going to have a departure off runway XZ.'Aircraft B responded 'I am in the air.'The tower replied 'Disregard; Land and hold short of runway XZ; land and hold short of runway XZ.'Aircraft B responded that this was their intention and would be parking in an area that would not put them at risk of crossing into runway XZ.The tower approved a request to taxi back to parking after Aircraft B completed a 180 degree turn on the runway after landing.30 seconds later the tower controller said to Aircraft B; 'Disregard the land and hold short clearance. I won't have that departure.  He will be holding in place; though.'The tower instructed Aircraft Y to line up and wait on runway XZ.The 737 had already landed on XXL and the tower cleared a Cessna for takeoff runway XXL.20 seconds later Aircraft B realized he was about to land on top of Aircraft A who had just been cleared for takeoff and asked the tower if he should go around.  There was no response.  Aircraft B hailed the tower again.  I observed Aircraft B descend below 100 ft AGL before deciding to go around.  40 seconds elapsed between the 1st and 3rd time Aircraft B called the tower.The tower gave the departing Aircraft A; a mixed up call starting with 'line up and- cancel take off- cleared for takeoff runway XXL'The tower then gave Aircraft B instructions to remain in the upwind; he would give him a crosswind instruction to follow.Aircraft B apologized for lining up to land on the wrong runway.As soon as the frequency congestion allowed; knowing there was a jet on the opposite side of my runway; I made a call 'Tower; Helicopter (call-sign) holding position on the numbers of [Runway] XY ready to taxi to (name of ramp)'.  The call was not acknowledged and 55 seconds later an amended departure clearance; combined with a takeoff clearance; was given to the waiting Aircraft Y.   I did not hear the departure clearance and Aircraft Y began racing towards us.  Ironically; I may have turned to my student and said to keep an eye on Aircraft Y.  As it rushed overhead I made an aggressive maneuver off of the numbers and onto the closest available vacant spot beyond the runway safety area.Previous experiences at this airport have made it clear when a helicopter accepts a landing clearance to a spot; taxiway; intersection; or helipad; they are expected to remain there until given a clearance to taxi.  Quite often the controllers will vector an arriving helicopter far around the approach or departure center lines of the active runways and restrict them to altitudes below 600 MSL instead of accommodating a flight path crossing the active runways at a higher safe altitude. Less often are we allowed to land as in the case above in a place safely away from the departing/arriving aircraft; and in a position where we can easily air taxi at a moment's notice.  A helicopter is highly maneuverable and this aspect should be used to the utmost advantage when minimizing delays to arriving or departing airplanes.  As mentioned earlier the helicopter's arrival was prior to Aircraft Z checking in with the tower.  There was Aircraft A on a half-mile final to runway XXL ahead of Aircraft Z.  With several miles of spacing between Aircraft Z and Aircraft A; the tower began to ask the helicopter to pass behind the landing Aircraft A.  We accepted.  The tower immediately reversed their decision due to Aircraft Z scheduled arrival and cleared us to land on the numbers of [Runway] XY with the restriction 'remain north of XX'. We accepted the clearance to land.  It is very likely that a helicopter crossing the approach end of XXL shortly after the landing Aircraft A would have had little to no effect on any of the other present arriving or departing aircraft.

column121: Early morning at roughly XA:30; Aircraft X flew from the west into ZZZ for pattern work. After completing three laps in the pattern an airport operations vehicle flagged down the pilot in command. The pilot in command then preceded to reject the takeoff and continue to the run up area. Airport operations advised the pilot to contact Tower at XXZ.A where the pilot was advised that he could continue pattern work yet had to take a phone number down. Pilot took down phone number and contacted Tower staff after the flight.Due to COVID-19 many ATC facilities are having to temporary close down due to cleaning. ZZZ has also been changing hours of ATC operation in the last ninety days. Pilots from ZZZ1 have also run into the problem of not properly reaching Air Traffic Control due to altered non-posted hours.The pilot in command flying was a student pilot that had recently soloed. When contacted by an airport operations vehicle; [they] only asked for intentions which the pilot responded that he was doing pattern work. At the time it could not be depicted if the airport operations vehicle told on XYY.Z to contact Tower on XXZ.A. In the future [if] airport operations could do this it would help. At the time the pilot thought the airport operations vehicle was attempting to do a FOD patrol of the runway since it was the early morning. The aircraft has been in the past known to have radio issues at random times.The student pilot will go over procedures with Class Delta airports with a flight instructor to mitigate problems in the future.

column121: I file this report for two reasons: to note a particular pilot's decision-making; and to talk about a larger potentially dangerous airport-environment situation.  Here is the relevant data:- The airport in question is Montgomery County Airpark; in Gaithersburg; Maryland; GAI. It is a very busy *uncontrolled* airport. It is within the DC SFRA; so pilots must obtain a discrete transponder code from Potomac Approach before taking off; and before re-entering the SFRA from outside. - The airport's only runway is 32/14; about 4000 feet long. The airport ATIS specifies that Runway 14 is preferred in calm-wind conditions. Also; the only approach to GAI is an RNAV/LPV approach to Runway 14. - There is a very; very active primary-training type airport. Nearly all of its students are [from] overseas; and the frequency of their flight means that the traffic-pattern at the airport is usually 'full.' It is typical to have one plane doing a runup; another taking off; another on downwind turning to base; and two or three others approaching from the north; all at the same time.- On the morning of this incident; winds had been in the 5 kt range--but from the north. So traffic through the morning had been all on Runway 32. - Now; the time in question. It was about XA:00 local EST. I was approaching from the north; and I received a code for entering the SFRA from Potomac Approach. As is usual practice; when I was about 12 miles north of GAI; I told Potomac; 'Gaithersburg in sight;' and they gave the formulaic response: 'Stay on discrete transponder code until landing; remain outside Class Bravo; switch to local frequency approved.' So I switched to the local UNICOM; 123.075.-I heard on the frequency what I also saw on my ADS-B display: That the pattern was; as usual; 'busy;' with three or four planes at various points in the circuit. And all of them were using Runway 32. (The winds at that moment were reporting calm on ATIS; but the pattern had been in steady use all day; on 32.)-Over the next eight minutes or so; between first radio contact and landing; I noticed two recurrent phenomena. One was many planes reporting their progress and position in a pattern for Runway 32.  I made calls; beginning at 8 miles out; with intentions to follow the established local practice. ('Forty-five to join right downwind for Runway 32.') The other notable entry was one airplane (Airplane X) that reported it was to the west; and 'straight in landing; Runway 14.'-A plane reports 'downwind 32.' Aircraft X says; 'straight in; Runway 14.' Another plane says; 'Aircraft X; we are using 32; please circle to land.' Aircraft pilot says; 'Straight in Runway 14.' At least twice; and I think three times; flight instructors say 'Aircraft X; PLEASE circle to land 32. We are all using 32.' Aircraft X replies; 'Straight in; 14.'-I kept reporting my own position; and said at one point 'Aircraft X; I am turning base to final for landing 32.' At that point I could see him descending to 14 -- i.e.; head on. The distances were such that it was clear to me that I could land safely and normally; and get off the runway; before he got too close.   And I proceeded to land. I turned off the runway halfway down; while he was still probably a mile out on opposite-direction final. All the other planes in the Runway 32 pattern extended their downwind etc.; to land. -The two planes landed at XA:07 pm EST; but in opposite directions.-Later; I saw someone who I assumed to be the Aircraft X pilot. He was; and I asked him: 'Why did you do that?' His answer was that he was fine-tuning the coupled-autopilot and wanted to fly an approach all the way down. -Note: I have been in this situation myself too; wanting to check out autopilots. But I choose airports where I can do so in keeping with the local traffic flow. -The main problem in this scenario was the Aircraft X pilot; who insisted on plowing ahead despite repeated requests on the frequency to switch to join the busy local traffic flow. I realize this is not an 'enforcement' forum; and I mention it just FYI.-The larger point is that the Gaithersburg airport has become unsustainably busy; for its uncontrolled status.  I have landed there probably X times over the past XX years. I *always* view the most challenging part of any trip to be the final 10 minutes of trying to fit into the uncontrolled but increasingly busy traffic pattern there.  With many primary students in training; they're often doing unexpected things in the pattern; or are uncertain in radio calls. Suggestion / request: Sooner or later there is going to be some safety incident at this airport; coming from too much traffic with too little control. A tower controller would *never* have allowed the situation I'm reporting to emerge. This is a problem waiting to happen at this airport.

column121: Approached ZZZ Runway XX for landing at approximately XA:50 from the south. After monitoring radio communications and no one in the pattern I made the decision to approach for landing straight in. I made a radio call stating my intentions and reporting 3 mile final for runway XX. I reduced throttle and speed to within flap range. I input flaps adjusted trim and further reduced speed. I turned on the runway lighting and adjusted course to the left then made a radio call for a mile final approach to runway XX. I verified my indicated airspeed was 62kts as I approached the runway; aimed for the numbers; and reminded myself the runway is closer than it appears in the dark. I then touched down hard on the runway and the nose of the aircraft bounced high sounding the stall warning. When the nose gear came back down in contact with the runway again it did not support the aircraft and the propeller came in contact with the runway stopping the aircraft on runway XX. My first concern was that I was obstructing the runway and tried to make a radio call. However; the radio was not working; at which point I powered down the aircraft and was attempting to open the canopy when I was approached by bystanders at the airport. They asked if I was okay and moved the aircraft off the runway via [Taxiway] 1A; by holding on to and lowering the tail pulling the aircraft on its main landing gear.

column121: I decided to do some practice approaches with my safety pilot. I got gas at ZZZ1 and it was a direct line from there for the approach into ZZZ so I did that one first. I got the weather; which was favoring the opposite direction; and changed to the advisory frequency. Another airplane announced that it was on the the approach for Runway XX but was farther out than we were. I announced that I was on the approach for Runway XY and would break off early. There was a lot of chatter on the radio both at ZZZ and at other airports that shared that frequency. We heard someone else mention Runway XX but couldn't make out what they were doing. I broke off the approach at about 800 ft. and 2 miles from the end of the runway as I knew I'd be far from the aircraft on the opposite approach. That's when my safety pilot saw the near miss plane that had departed Runway XX at some point. We never heard them announce taking off or on upwind and they did not show up on ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast). We immediately turned left for the missed but were past them by that point. After we passed them and announced the missed; the pilot of the other aircraft said something on the radio that I couldn't make out.Contributing factors were me continuing an approach in the wrong direction longer than I should have given the heavy chatter on the radio. The other aircraft was also not announcing enough or not announcing correctly or getting stepped on by other chatter or otherwise unintelligible. Another contributing factor was the other aircraft not having ADS-B Out installed. It wasn't required there but it would have greatly helped avoid the near miss. Given that we did hear another mention of Runway XX; I should have asked for their position since I didn't hear it the first time. In the future; I will break off opposite direction approaches much sooner when there is other traffic in the vicinity.

column121: During a tailwheel transition training flight; the aircraft departed the runway surface on landing. The winds upon time of landing favored Runway XX and a right-crosswind component of about 10 knots was present at the time of the occurrence. No other traffic was in the pattern and the approach was stable throughout. The touchdown was in a three point attitude and did not bounce. On the rollout; the student improperly managed rudder control and the aircraft rapidly developed a significant turn to the left. As Instructor; I took control of the aircraft and stopped the ground loop from further developing. The aircraft departed the hard surface of the runway at roughly a 10 degree angle at a fairly slow speed and came to rest in the grass about 20 feet from the edge of the runway. Upon shutting the airplane down; both the student and I exited the airplane to assess the situation. No signage or lighting was hit nor was there any damage present on the airplane. The grass was smooth and no holes were present.The situation developed from a normal crosswind landing to a runway excursion quickly. The cause was an improper control input by the student that was not caught in time by me; the instructor. Despite not reacting in time to prevent the excursion; the aircraft did not ground loop and no damage was sustained by the airplane. Any corrective action would be on my part as the Instructor; to take control sooner before such a significant turn could develop.

column121: This was my first flight at the controls of a tail wheel aircraft. I was in the left seat receiving flight instruction from the CFI in the right seat. A thorough pre-takeoff briefing including experience levels and positive transfer of controls was accomplished before departure.As we approached ZZZ; we briefed the fact there was a right crosswind with gusts and the appropriate actions to take regarding this. The approach was stabilized. A normal wheel landing was accomplished and the tail was successfully lowered to the ground. The left main tire failed; at which point the instructor stated 'my airplane' and I released the controls. The resulting swerve was not controllable and the airplane ground looped approximately 150 degrees; coming to rest on the runway. We immediately shut down the aircraft and exited. No propeller or wingtip contact with the runway occurred. The aircraft remained on the runway. No injuries occurred.
column123: The mission was to fly with 2 friends and give them tail wheel instruction. There was a crosswind from the right and we discussed crosswind correction and the plan. [The pilot flying] conducted the wheel landing and shortly after putting the tail down; the airplane started shaking violently. I thought this may have initially been a tail wheel shimmy; which was odd since it didn't shimmy since the tail wheel springs were replaced in month; but the airplane started veering to the left so I announced 'my controls' and corrected it with right rudder. The shaking got worse and the plane then swung around to the right and ground looped. The wings did not contact the surface and there was no prop strike. The airplane was then towed to the hangar where I worked with a mechanic to change the wheel and tire so that the plane could be moved while inside the hangar. I did identify some contributing factors. There was a strong right crosswind; it was my student's first landing; and I had previous issues with my tires slipping on grooved runways. They are 8.50 oversize tires. I do believe the left main tire went flat on landing; and with the strong crosswind and delay of taking the controls from my student; it was unrecoverable. I'm filling out this report to detail human factors issues that contributed to damage to my precious airplane; and as the investigation unfolds it will determine if there is need for additional caution when using larger tires.

column121: After two right 360s we were told to extend downwind for runway X; and look for helicopter traffic (Aircraft Y) three miles west of the field at 700 feet. We called out traffic in sight; and continued. After Aircraft Y didn't respond to two radio calls; we were told to do another 360. Rolling out of the 360 we were told to look for Aircraft Y one mile ahead at 900 feet orbiting. We called traffic in sight; and began a climb to 1;300 feet. It appeared as though Aircraft Y was still climbing as they passed in front from our left to right. After a controller change; Tower called our position to Aircraft Y; they did not respond. Shortly after that call; Aircraft Y made a sharp climbing right turn directly into our flight path. To avoid a collision; I took the controls and made a climbing left turn as sharp as I could. Shortly after I started that turn; Aircraft Y banked sharply to their right to avoid us. I can't put an exact number on the distance between us; but it was close enough that I felt the need to bank sharply towards traffic on final; and Aircraft Y banked hard enough for us to see the bottom of their helicopter. Once a safe distance away; we turned to rejoin downwind; and began a descent back to pattern altitude. After that; Aircraft Y asked tower to keep aircraft away from that area while they followed a pursuit. Hearing other aircraft have difficulty with separation; we departed the pattern to ZZZ1 to avoid a similar situation.It is normal for us to fly over helicopter operations at 500-600 feet while in the pattern at 1;100 feet. It is not normal to fly the pattern with unpredictable traffic at the same altitude.

column121: Flight originated in ZZZ as a Part 135 scheduled flight to ZZZ1. There were no passengers on board.  ZZZ Center advised us that ZZZ4 Center would be going to an 'ATC Zero' condition for 1 hour 30 minutes at 15 minutes prior to our scheduled arrival due to a COVID situation in the Center facility. I made the decision to divert to ZZZ3 and accomplished training enroute and landing late afternoon. Weather in ZZZ3 was IFR with a report that fog was believed to be moving into the ZZZ3 area. We refueled and departed for ZZZ1. Training was again accomplished enroute...landing was at night with 2;500 broken; 3;100 overcast and 3 mile in R and BR. This was the end of a long day that started early morning for a departure to ZZZ5 from ZZZ1...scheduled time was 1 hour 50 minutes with a 20 minute turn. Due to waiting for a dead heading crew member we left ZZZ5 one hour late; arriving ZZZ1 at noon. I picked up another FO and departed for ZZZ for a planned 1 hour 40 minute flight. Landing at ZZZ; we then departed for a planned 1 hour 40 minute flight to ZZZ1. As noted previously; we were forced to divert to ZZZ3; due to ATC Zero. I exceeded 8 hours but; felt that; per our FOM and the FARs; I was legal to start and finish because the divert to ZZZ3 was not planned and the scheduled times were within legal limits. Note that I had over 14 hours rest before the flying the following day and was off duty after the days flying was complete and no other flying scheduled for several days.The issue that bothers me is that I was accomplishing training at night and in solid IMC conditions...never again. There was some unspoken pressure to get the training accomplished due to approaching holiday and a lack of aircraft to accomplish the training during daylight hours. I also should not have pressed the flying...the start of the problem was the unplanned ZZZ5 turn due to the scheduled Captain timing out and for whom I was asked to cover. As soon as we knew we would have to divert to ZZZ3; I should have terminated any further training and proceeded to ZZZ1 as soon as ZZZ4 Center re-opened. Several 'takeaways'...I will not allow this to happen to me again; even though I believed (and believe) I was legal...fatigue was not an issue. Training should only be accomplished in solid VMC conditions and preferably in daylight.

column121: Aircraft X came to an abrupt stop on Runway XX at ZZZ due to snow on the runway. We were the only occupants of the craft. Neither of us were injured; nor was the plane damage. There was no damage to any other persons or property.A low approach was made to assess the condition of the runway before attempting a soft field approach and landing. We decided to make an approach to land after judging that the snow looked to be at or less than 2 inches. It looks like two layers of very thin snow. We could see tracks from another tricycle gear airplane. What we didn't realize was that that plane had landed in much shallower snow and that it had then snowed more on top. Being able to see grass protruding through the snow also gave the notion that the snow was not deep. I briefed my student on precautions to take with landing on snow before we made the approach.When we landed; the plane's mains and nose wheel sunk in causing us to come to an abrupt halt. We were able to taxi the aircraft most of the way up the runway. We agreed to attempt a soft field take off back down our tracks; which didn't get very far.Chief; Assistant Chief; Owner; and Lead Pilot were notified. We contacted the Airport Manager; who was able to come to our aid with a backhoe. We took off from the county road next to the runway as decided between myself; the Student and Chief Pilot; and as advised by the Airport Manager. A successful short field takeoff and climb out was performed by myself; the instructor and my student and I returned to ZZZ1.14 CFR 91.103; Pre-flight preparation; was not observed or fulfilled to its fullest. I will not get into the possible reasoning behind this; aside from that we decided to go to #X# during taxi.Lessons learned are abundant by our main takeaways that [we] I discussed were as follows:-New or unfamiliar airports need better preparation and scrutiny.-Snow depth should not be judged from the air. Until properly equipped and properly trained; no approach and landing should be made to a snowy runway that one is not sure they could take off from again.-I now have a new example of things not to do to use as a teaching tool with my students.We were extremely lucky pilots today. but we as pilots do not want to rely on luck. Lessons learned.

column121: It has been hard to fly during the pandemic; and the aircraft had been in for annual inspection; so I had not flown for two months. I went out for practice. I chose the back-course approach at ZZZ; as it can be challenging. Also; during recurrent training in Month; we had noticed some odd autopilot behavior when flying this approach. My aircraft has Garmin avionics but these are mated to an older analogue autopilot.By the time I was told to switch to ZZZ1 Approach; I was still at 12;000 feet and quite close to ZZZZZ intersection on the approach. When I gave my request for the approach; the controller gave me vectors to circle back to rejoin the course while descending to 4000 feet. She then cleared me for the approach. I believed she said 'Maintain 4000 until established...'; but in our later discussion she said her instruction was 'Maintain 4000 to ZZZZZ.' I believe I read back the former. In any case; when back on extended approach course; but a short distance before ZZZZZ; I began to descend further. The chart showed 3000 feet for the segment between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1; which is the FAF and 5.8NM from ZZZZZ. My GPS displayed an altitude of 3100 at ZZZZZ; which I believe is its indication of a safe altitude. So; I had set altitude capture for 3100 feet and was descending. The controller alerted me that she had expected 4000 feet to ZZZZZ. While we were discussing this; the autopilot failed to capture and the descent continued to 2900 feet. The controller told me to switch to tower.On my first attempt to call tower at ZZZ; I had not hit the switch correctly and was still with ZZZ1 approach. At the same time; I noticed the autopilot taking me off course for the approach and interrupted it while calling the tower. We were in the descent within the FAF by this time. The tower controller told me I was low for the course and left of course; and he asked if I was flying the approach visually instead of using the Back Course. Due to the autopilot issue; I was by that time flying visually. It was a clear VFR day; and at no time was I in close proximity to terrain or other aircraft. The problem arose for several reasons. The pilot (me) was rusty and needed practice. It was a mistake to do the more challenging BC approach as the first one. (After this event; I did the missed approach as planned at ZZZ and did two fine approaches at ZZZ1 and ZZZ2.) Also; I believe there anomalies with my avionics set-up and back-course approaches; and I should not have been trying to troubleshoot that as a single pilot; especially being a bit out of practice. Another contributor was my misunderstanding of the controller's instruction; along with using the 3000 foot altitude indicated on the chart for that segment ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1) and the 3100 foot altitude indicated as the target for ZZZZZ on my GPS for the altitude I was trying to attain. All of these issues increased workload; which is better handled by an in-practice pilot (which is why I had gone out to practice). A final recommendation from this experience is that I will avoid flying BC approaches with my autopilot until I can do a flight with a competent pilot and avionics technician aboard. The BC approaches are quite rare; and almost all have GPS overlays nowadays. So; they are not really a high priority; I actually chosen this one to be challenging and give me practice monitoring the autopilot and taking over if it acted strangely. But given the altitude misunderstanding; resulting discussion; and then the strange autopilot behavior; it was a bit choppy. I flew the airplane in a safe manner throughout (there was no terrain issue along my path); but my adherence to published instructed and published altitudes on the approach was poor.

column123: We were practicing short field landings for training. After landing the student started applying brakes very lightly. The tail began to rise and I applied full aft elevator to help slow the rise but was unable to prevent the prop from striking the runway. From the time aggressive brakes were applied until the prop struck the ground was less than .5 seconds. I had previously briefed with the student what the appropriate short field landing and braking action should look like on the ground and in flight just before the demonstration. I then demonstrated how the maneuver was to be performed before allowing the student to execute the maneuver. Total distance covered from the time the prop impacted the runway was only approximately 5 feet. After the aircraft came to a stop I shut everything down besides the radio; made a radio call to traffic in the area to temporarily close the runway and then had the student monitor the radios while I contacted airport management to notam the runway closed and get assistance with the aircraft. A preliminary inspection revealed damage to the prop; spinner; and lower cowling. No injuries were incurred and not further damage is known at this time.

column121: I departed ZZZ East ramp in [a] R22 with a private pilot student for pre-solo training at ZZZ1. We practiced emergency procedures en-route. After listening to ZZZ1 ASOS we determined to set up to enter the traffic pattern for Runway XX. 8 miles west from ZZZ1 we announced our location on CTAF and identified there were two airplanes in the pattern. We entered a 45 degree left downwind for Runway XX at ZZZ1 at 1;100 ft. and 75 kts. We announced and turned left base for Runway XX at 900 ft. and 60 kts. during which I could see Aircraft Y in a close left downwind. We announced turning final and turned final on Runway XX rolling out at 300 ft. AGL (900 ft. MSL) and 60 kts. I instructed the student to perform a normal approach to the approach end of Runway XX and terminate to a 3 ft. hover directly over the numbers (just as would be required during solo or a check ride). The student initiated his normal approach at the normal 10 degree angle required. I then heard Aircraft Y announce he was on final for Runway XX and had the helicopter in sight. I assumed the airplane had misjudged his spacing in the traffic pattern would either adjust his airspeed; perform turns for spacing; or go around. This is not uncommon and simple courtesy to the lower aircraft. On short final for Runway XX I looked out the left rear of the helicopter and could see Aircraft Y on short final right behind us. Aircraft Y asked me my intentions on CTAF. I replied that I intended to complete a landing to a hover at the approach end of Runway XX and then conduct a normal takeoff. Three things were on my mind. First; an aircraft on final and at a lower altitude always has the right of way. Second; I wanted the student to have the opportunity to conduct a normal approach to a hover just as he will be required to do during upcoming solo flight and his PPL checkride. Third; I need to access the student's ability to terminate the landing to a stationary hover. I asked Aircraft Y if he intended to 'go around' as it was clear either we would have to rush off the runaway; before completing the landing; or Aircraft Y could go-around. Aircraft X immediately replied with a complaint over CTAF stating that 'you little black helicopters are hogging the runways here and as a local pilot I can tell you that we are sick of you'. Just as I decelerated to a 3 ft. hover over the numbers for Runway XX I heard the sound of an airplane at high rpm overhead. I looked up to see Aircraft X directly over my helicopter about 20-30 ft. As he overflew me; he stated; 'he intended to report me to the FAA' and requested my name. I provided my tail number for his use as I did not want to provide my name over CTAF. I then contacted Aircraft Y over CTAF and requested that he not over fly my aircraft (for fear of collision) and that I will work with him to gain proper spacing in the pattern. Aircraft Y insulted me over CTAF and challenged me to a physical altercation. I instructed the student hover taxi to the parallel taxiway for Runway XX. I then noticed a pickup truck [surveying] our helicopter. I instructed the student to land on a nearby taxiway intersection near parking and go to idle. I exited the helicopter and approach the truck. I greeted the driver of the white truck with a handshake; introduced myself; and asked if there was an issue. I was told by the driver that they are reporting me to the FAA and they are just 'sick of our little helicopters that are difficult to see and tie up the runways for airplanes.' I sympathized with the driver but told him this is a public airport and that we have a right to conduct flight training here just as much as anyone; provided we all adhere to the rules. Furthermore; I told him that the airplane made an error in spacing by turning downwind; base; and final too quickly and essentially attempted to push me off the runway while conducting a landing. I told the driver that I am sorry this happened; but I feel the airplane did not adhere to Part 91 Right of Way rules to a lower aircraft on final. I gave the driver my number and told him I'd be more than happy to work with him on any future issues. We shook hands and went separate ways. I returned to the helicopter and returned directly to ZZZ. My chief concern with this incident is that the airplane should not have rushed or crowded another aircraft on final approach. A change in speed; turns for spacing; or a go-around were all options for the airplane pilot. Furthermore; executed a go around directly over and in close proximity to another aircraft is dangerous. What if I had directed the student to execute a go around or immediate takeoff (because we were being rushed on final and had climbed up into the airplane. As a military aviator and civilian helicopter and airplane pilot of over XX years I had always striven to fly with the utmost safety and friendliness. I preach this to my students; and I hope that all Aviators practice this as well. My goal is simply to encourage friendly; smart; and safe flying by all pilots at both ZZZ and ZZZ1.

column121: I was conducting a training flight with a student and entered the pattern at PWT on the 45 for a full stop landing on Runway 20; making all radio calls in the pattern. As I was on short final (100 ft. AGL); the aircraft holding short makes a radio call that he is 'taking the active [Runway] 20'. He did not move his aircraft and continued holding short as I crossed the threshold; at which point I assumed he saw me as I passed right in front of his windshield in my roundout. I could not make any radio calls within those few seconds due to other traffic making calls in the pattern. As I am completing my landing roll to exit on taxiway A3; I hear a plane takeoff right on top of me. I asked on CTAF if he took off while I was still on the runway; to which 3 different aircraft concurred that he did. After a few minutes; as I'm departing the airspace; the aircraft in the pattern (along with myself) were discussing the events that transpired over radio. At that point; the pilot in question keyed up saying 'I'm still on frequency guys; what's the problem?'. I told him that he took off while I was still on the runway; to which he replied 'yeah; what's the problem with that?'. Another pilot noted that immediately after lift-off; he executed a steep right turn and exited the airspace at low level. In my professional opinion; the actions of the PIC of Aircraft X is a textbook example of a reckless operation; and a clear demonstration of several different hazardous attitudes. He obviously showed no remorse for his actions; believing that they were considered 'normal' things to do. There was absolutely nothing I could have done to prevent this from happening; because it is clearly all happening from the other guy's end. If I had to execute a go-around; it would almost definitely have resulted in a midair collision. The only way to prevent something like this from happening again is remedial training for this guy; or even a reevaluation of his certificate; because the way he operates his aircraft is clearly without regard for anyone's safety.

column121: During this incident I was on a checkride and we ran a partial panel VOR Runway X approach with a circle to Runway XY. This is normally a Class D airspace but the Tower at ZZZ is currently closed due to COVID and this has presented some challenges to the arriving and departing process given we share the airport with airline operations. We made it to the left downwind for XY and there was a carrier aircraft holding short of XY getting ready to take the runway and they requested over CTAF for us to extend our downwind so they could takeoff. We extended our downwind about a mile or so and decided to turn base. About the time we were turning base there was another carrier that called a 10 mile final for XY. With the position report given; we were under the impression we had the appropriate spacing for us to get on the ground and off the runway before they reached the field. We continued and turned in for final and the carrier taking off was on the roll. I made position reports and heard nothing back that would indicate an issue. When we were on short final carrier made a 6 mile final call. I then made a position call for short final and we were within a half mile of landing. About the time I was roughly 100 feet over the runway threshold; the carrier aircraft called and stated; 'Aircraft on short final; we are going around and will be flying above you.' We landed safely and had to extend our ground roll down the runway to exit because another carrier aircraft was taxiing to Runway XY via Taxiway A and we had to taxi beyond where they were. That concludes the incident. I do not know how accurate the position reports were from carrier or their speed but there didn't appear to be an issue on spacing and if they knew they were catching us that fast they could have let us know and I would have executed a go-around. This was not a near-miss event and we never saw the aircraft near us on ADS-B radar or receive any traffic notification. It seems to be more lack of communication in a non-towered environment with busy airspace as a root cause. I think they were well aware of our location in front of them and didn't speak up to let us know how quick they were catching us. I feel like there should be some additional measures in place when a tower is closed at an airport like this with heavier volume and many different types and sizes of aircraft operating. Sharing an airport between GA and airline ops in a non-towered environment is setting the stage for incidents like this to happen and truly presents some added challenges and hazards.

column121: In the traffic pattern at ZZZ; my CFI and I were on the right downwind for Runway XXR when we were told to Continue for Runway XXR. We then continued and a few moments later was told to turn right base for XXR. When turning right base we noted traffic; but I didn't think it was a factor at first because we assumed it was for the parallel because we still were told to turn right base.  As we got established on base we saw the traffic was close and my CFI took controls to avoid a mid-air collison. We got no warning from the Tower and later found out that the tower told the other aircraft to continue for Runway XXR. Shortly after the Tower told them to continue for XXR that's when the tower said to turn base. I didn't think that traffic that was on final would be a factor for us and thought it was for Runway XXL. In the future; I think the Tower should be more clear and understand the traffic spacing better because if he did then he could've told us to extend a couple of miles so we could've passed behind the traffic instead of passing in front and coming within 1;000 feet horizontally of each other. I believe the talking between me and my CFI also contributed because maybe we would've heard the call for the other aircraft to continue and could've challenged that with the Tower but even then we still were told to turn base. I believe the tower should've noted the other aircraft and looked at the spacing; and told us this isn't going to work and this near-miss could've been avoided altogether instead we got turned directly into the path of another aircraft.
column123: I was flying with my student in the pattern at ZZZ. When we were downwind; Tower didn't clear us for a touch and go; but told us to continue. We continued downwind and waited for further instructions when Tower then told us to turn base.We turned base. There was some hesitation but then the Controller instructed us to turn directly towards the numbers. At this point; we were on right base unaware we were being turned onto an aircraft that was on final.   Before my students turn for final; I always have them look on final to make sure it is clear of traffic. At this point; I noticed the traffic on the left hand side and saw it on my iPad. I took the controls from my student and climbed to offset to the right where we avoided a near miss collision of about 1;000 feet horizontal distance and 300 feet vertical distance over a densely packed neighborhood of City. We never were told to extend or follow this aircraft.Prior to the Controller telling us to turn base; he had spoken to the aircraft on the straight in final and told them to continue. He realized the aircraft was there; but did not communicate the location and told us to turn base onto him. This situation demonstrates that pilots must exercise extreme vigilance at airports where ATC is so busy to provide clear instructions.The term 'continue' can be vague in that…does it mean we're supposed to fly the pattern as regularly; or are we supposed to continue downwind? In that case; the term 'extend' would make more sense.When I talked to the Controller on the phone later; I was told that this situation occurred due to a late runway switch by the other aircraft. However; in examination of the track log; the aircraft was on a straight in approach. The pilot also called up that they were approaching a point on the approach for XXR.  The Controller didn't acknowledge the mistake that had been made and the possible deadly consequences that could have occurred from this near miss.This is a serious near miss.

The student at the controls was 2-3 seconds late in beginning the glideslope intercept; and our glideslope indicated slightly high. Knowing that we had to descend 500 feet in order to be below the upcoming 7;000 feet MSL Class B shelf; I reduced power to increase our rate of descent. There was also an air carrier [Aircraft Y] at our 1 o'clock; approximately 1;000 feet above our altitude according to ADS-B; which was making a right turn from a southerly heading to a northwesterly as it make its approach to DEN. Denver Approach contacted us saying; 'I need you below the Bravo shelf at 7;000 feet.' I replied 'roger; we are increasing our rate of descent; currently indicating 6;800 feet.' The Aircraft Y crossed above and ahead of us; right to left; approximately 1;000 feet above and 200 feet ahead. I did not hear any of the communications between the Aircraft Y and Denver Approach; nor did I notice any maneuvering by the Aircraft Y indicating it was reacting to our presence. The complex airspace around DEN is extremely challenging; and this approach's FAF is approximately 1.4 NM from the 7;000 feet MSL Class B shelf. Descending 500 feet in less than 1.4 NM at small aircraft approach speeds does not require excessive rates of descent; but it does require a timely descent. Any delay; or crossing the FAF above the 7;500 feet MSL altitude; quickly makes it likely that an airplane may violate Class B airspace during the Final Approach Segment. In our case; the timing of the arriving Aircraft Y was coincidentally exactly the same time we were at this critical place. As a CFI-I; I am reluctant to use this approach for training ever again. One suggestion may be to cross ARRES at an altitude lower than the charted minimum of 7;500 feet MSL - if; and only if; it's a practice approach under VFR. The potential negative training this would cause would have to be weighed against the extra margin of separation from the Class B shelf. Additionally; in the future; if I use this approach for practice again; I will have the student execute a missed approach and turn away from the 7;000 feet MSL Class B shelf if the aircraft is high at ARRES; does not initiate a timely descent; or if I notice DEN traffic that could cross above us as happened on this flight.

The King Air's TCAS system showed that we reached within 100 feet of each other but myself and the pilots in the King Air agreed that it was much more that 100 feet. I could have been more watchful of my track to stay clear of final. The winds were from the northwest so that could have been a factor in why I was slightly drifting. That is why it is important to know where your winds are coming from to maintain a constant ground track along the ground and prevent drifting.

column121: Upon reaching clearance for ILS XX circle Runway XY at ZZZ from Approach; we were switched over to ZZZ Tower frequency. I broke off from the approach and turned to the south; since we were no longer receiving navigational guidance along the approach; and I had no communications to contact Tower or Approach. No indications of ammeter discharge or low voltage illuminated; and the turn coordinator was still operable as well as engine instruments; so I presumed that the failure was based solely on avionics and not complete electrical failure. We descended lower; maintaining VFR so that we could receive cell signal; and I contacted ZZZ Tower via cellphone; since they gave us instructors their phone number another time when they had an ATC/instructor meeting. I told them we were okay; and had complete avionics failure. I asked for the phone number for ZZZ1 Tower so I could communicate with them if I decided to continue south to ZZZ1. At that time; the visibility and clouds around ZZZ began to clear up and we could start to see towards ZZZ. I asked ZZZ Tower if the field was still IFR; and they replied that it just went VFR. We proceeded inbound toward ZZZ; maintaining VFR; and were able to receive landing and taxi clearances for our aircraft through the cell phone. The aircraft was repaired; with the problem being a short-circuited avionics switch.

column121: This was my third solo XC (Cross Country). Flight planning was approved by the instructor. Weather and NOTAMs were reviewed by both myself and instructor and flight was deemed safe to proceed. There were no NOTAMs or field condition reports for the destination airport. One pattern was flown at departure airport with an instructor to update currency prior to departure of solo flight. Takeoff; climb; en route; and descent were uneventful. During a visual approach to Runway 02 at the uncontrolled airport; I noticed patchy snow on the runway. I noticed other aircraft had landed recently. I was expecting a normal landing to a touch and go. ASOS indicated the winds were from the northwest at 8 kts. I touched down on centerline at 67 kts. Before I set the nose down; the aircraft started veering to the left. I made the attempt to correct and the airplane continued to slide to the left. I believe due to the unresponsiveness of my control inputs; I was on ice. I made the decision to full stop and applied brakes. The aircraft continued to slide on the icy portion of the runway with no response to my braking or control inputs. The aircraft struck a snow bank on the left side of the runway. The aircraft tipped forward and to the right; resulting in damage to the propeller and the right wingtip. I'm not sure if this is a reportable incident/accident at this time. The following day; a NOTAM was issued for 30 PCT patchy snow and ice.	I believe I landed on a patch of ice. There were no NOTAMs published at the time of my departure. Had a NOTAM been published for wintery conditions; I would not have attempted a solo XC to this airport. I have not yet been trained to land in wintery conditions. Based on previous landing markings on the snow in the runway; I assumed it was safe to land. My relative inexperience resulted in not recognizing the ice under the snow. I should've gone around. In the future; I will take a harder look at my experience level and the conditions present in order to make a better decision. I have learned a valuable lesson to always err on the side of caution.

column121: I am a CFI and I was flying a training mission with my client who is a licensed private pilot working on transition training to a new model aircraft (Aircraft X). This was my client's first flight in a Aircraft X. The lesson started with a detailed preflight; followed by a similarly detailed run-up. Once ready; we departed Palo Alto Airport for a familiarization flight in a practice area south and west of the airport. During our time in the practice area we maintained visual separation from another aircraft in the training area (each trying to stay in our own section of the training area; while we also maintained appropriate distances from scattered clouds in the area; and staying below the Bravo which starts at 4;000 in that area. During this time; we stayed in contact with the Tower having asked them for advisories during our training mission.After approximately 1 hour of Hobbs time (including the taxi and detailed run-up); we copied ATIS Quebec and informed the Tower that we would like to return to the field for the option; and closed traffic. We were instructed to fly over Stanford and enter the pattern for left traffic for Runway 31. We made our way as instructed and entered the left downwind for Runway 31. The Tower then told us that we were number 4 cleared to land; and that the traffic that we were following was roughly abeam us in the opposite downwind. We acknowledged the instruction and reported negative contact with the traffic to follow. Meanwhile; the Tower was very busy with numerous other traffic entering; leaving; and in the pattern. We were then told to extend our downwind; that we had extensive extensions into Moffett Field's airspace (it is very common for Palo Alto to have and use extensions into Moffett's airspace - this extension was even further than usual) and that the Tower would call our base. While extending; we saw our traffic to follow turn base and then final. But we continued downwind since the Tower said that they would call our base.Moments later; the Tower instructed us to fly 'straight towards the 31 numbers' which was a bit strange since we were so far from the runway (probably at least 3 miles at this point). But the frequency was very busy and it didn't seem to make sense (or even possible) to ask to verify the instruction. We turned left onto a long final and proceeded towards the runway. We were holding approximately 1;000 feet (+/- since my student was flying and this was their first time in the aircraft) this entire time on downwind; base and long final.Not too long after we turned long final; the Tower told us to climb 500 feet immediately for traffic. I immediately took the controls of the plane; quickly (re)checked nearby traffic on the G1000 MFD (with ADS-B traffic) and did a visual scan for traffic as I went full forward on the throttle; prop; and mixture and pitched the nose back for the climb. The quick scan of traffic (visual and ADS-B) did not indicate any traffic below or next to us; but it did indicate one aircraft above our altitude but not in the immediate vicinity. None-the-less; we tried to visually acquire the above traffic as we climbed.Moments later; the tower told us to stop our climb immediately and to turn right and fly directly towards Leslie Salt. Again; we immediately complied with the Tower's instructions as we continued to try to acquire and track any immediate threats visually. Just then; we saw another aircraft pass directly above us; slightly off to our left side; in very close proximity to our aircraft. The Tower then instructed us to make a right turn back to final for landing.I've been flying at PAO for nearly XX years; so I am familiar with how busy it can get. But even with that experience; it was particularly busy at this time. One of the things that I think was a factor in this situation was a partial callsign conflict. Our aircraft callsign ended in [--] while the callsign of another aircraft on frequency at the time ended in [--]. In fact; it is possible that the aircraft above us when we were instructed to climb; and the one that nearly collided with moments later; was the aircraft ending in [--]. My theory is that the instruction to climb was actually intended for Aircraft Y and not Aircraft X; and that the controller tried to stop our climb as soon as he noticed the error. Unfortunately; these problems were all compounded by the heavy radio traffic making it virtually impossible to verify instructions; especially in a timely fashion.My client and I replayed this whole incident both while still in the air; and during debrief on the ground; and we are both quite certain that we responded to our correct callsign and that this wasn't a case of us improperly (and unintentionally) responding to someone else's callsign. I wanted to use the G1000 PLAYback feature to check/verify the radio call; but; unfortunately; the radio traffic was so heavy that there was no way to use the replay feature successfully. I have replayed this entire situation a number of times trying to analyze what I could have / should have done differently to avoid getting this close to another aircraft. Unfortunately; I haven't really come up with a good answer given the details of the situation.Given that the only nearby traffic that I could observe at the time was the one above us; I could have held my attitude of 1;000 feet; in defiance of the Tower Controller's instruction; until I could verify that the climb instruction was for us; or until I could verify another nearby traffic threat. But this seems like a very bad idea. I have always operated that when ATC gives you an immediate traffic avoidance instruction that you follow that instruction immediately. There could have very well been another nearby aircraft that I was unaware of that was an even more of a threat that I was currently unaware of. Hence my immediate response as instructed.I believe that the similar sounding callsigns; heavy radio traffic; and large number of aircraft operating in the class Delta; all contributed to the confusion for all parties. I know that it made our task (mine and my client) much more difficult; and I believe that you could hear that in the voice and instructions of the Tower Controller and the other pilots. After landing; we opted to terminate rather than continue pattern operations. Once back in the flying club; we talked with another CFI and student who was flying (and returning to the airport) at the same time. I asked them if they heard the Tower 'trying kill us' and the CFIs response was 'yeah; the Tower Controller was clearly overwhelmed!' We asked him if he heard any indications that we responded to the wrong callsign. His response was 'no' and that; again; he thought that whole problem was that the Tower Controller was simply overwhelmed by the overall situation.I know that Palo Alto is an FAA Training Tower; and I'm fully understanding and supportive of that. But perhaps in this case maybe there should have been additional oversight of Tower operations; or at least a senior controller stepping in before the controller got too overwhelmed.

column121: My student and I were returning to the home airport from the local practice area after a training flight. Since this was the student's 2nd training flight; I was explaining the correct traffic pattern entry and radio calls to him. I made the initial radio call 10 miles away from the airport and stated location; altitude and intentions. A short time later; a Mooney checked on to the CTAF and announced his location and intentions. I noted to myself that the Mooney was near us; but behind and decided to be vigilant. The wind favored landings on Runway XX that day; which meant that we would have to fly from the practice area to the northwest of the airport to an area southwest of the airport in order to make the 45 degree entry to the right traffic. I was a bit concerned as the student and I were flying in a Cessna 150 which is very slow and was worried about being overtaken by the faster Mooney as we both set up for the traffic pattern entry. I made my next radio call at a location approximately 4-5 miles northwest of the airport and stated that we intended to maneuver for the 45 degree entry to the traffic pattern. I also directed the student to descend to traffic pattern altitude. I continued to visually scan for the Mooney. Since I expected the Mooney to overtake us and since the right of way rules state that overtaking aircraft should pass on the right; I spent most of my time searching on our right. The pilot of the Mooney made a radio call and stated a position and distance from the airport that was very similar to ours. I became even more concerned about the possibility for a collision and made an additional radio call with our revised position and stated that we were in a Cessna 150; in an attempt to inform the Mooney pilot of our speed and the possibility for collision. The pilot of the Mooney made another radio call and stated his position; which was very similar to ours; 5 miles west of the airport. I became very concerned about the situation and began to aggressively scan for them. I didn't feel that it would be appropriate to divert towards the airport; as it would cause me to conflict with the traffic pattern. I also didn't feel that it would be appropriate to divert away from the airport; as I expected the Mooney to pass on the right. A very short time later; the Mooney passed by us on our left and slightly above us. It appeared to me that we were vertically separated by less than 200 feet and laterally separated by less than 200 feet.I realized after the fact; that I had allowed myself to continue into the possibility of a collision because I felt I had the right of way as the slower aircraft and because I did not want to cause my student an undue expense of maneuvering away from the airport. I noted that the other pilot made three radio calls that expressed essentially the same position and distance from the airport; yet I made no attempt to escape the situation. In the future; I will be more aggressive about maneuvering out of or away from potential traffic pattern conflicts.

column121: I am a private pilot; multi-engine student. I was working with my instructor on a variety of things that morning in the practice area. We came back to the airport and proceeded to perform some touch and go landings on Runway XX; left traffic. We performed two touch and go landings; then a full stop landing. We taxied back and performed two more touch and go landings before the tower asked us to switch to right traffic (five landings in total). On downwind; the nose gear light didn't come on immediately. The hydraulic lever would kick back telling us it was pressurized and I had visual confirmation that the front gear was down.We performed three more touch and go landings to do our best to confirm that the gear was down and locked. I recall the nose gear light would flicker from time to time. We performed the checklist items accordingly but could not get the nose light to stay on when extending the gear. Every time the hydraulic gear lever would return to neutral and the gear was visible in the mirror.  My instructor requested to the tower that we switch to the non active Runway (XY) so that he could land and get out to see what was going on with the gear. With the instructor flying; he chose to feather the left engine after the gear was lowered. No flaps were used. Upon landing; he shutdown the right engine. The plane initially acted normal but started to veer to the right as we continued down the runway. I could feel that he had very little directional control. He also has no brakes on the right seat position so he yelled 'left brake!; left brake!' I pushed the left brake as hard as I could and the plane turned left enough to stay on the runway; however shortly thereafter the nose gear collapsed. We skidded to a stop; shut everything down and exited the plane. The right engine hadn't stopped in time so the prop was damaged from contacting the runway. The left engine was feathered so there didn't appear to be any damage to it. The plane was removed from the non active runway and brought back to the hangar. I have no idea what we could have done differently as we had hydraulic pressure and visual confirmation that the gear was down (bad switch?). The previous touch and go landings were fine with no adverse steering issues. Perhaps the nose gear wasn't getting a lot of contact during the touch and goes but I still had directional control prior to him landing. Feathering the left engine obviously saved that from damage. The intent was to only gently land and inspect prior to taxing back to the hangar; but due to other circumstances the plane veered right; was corrected with left brake and the nose gear still ended up collapsing.

column121: During a routine training session of multi-engine student instruction on DATE; we experienced nose gear indication problems which terminated with a collapsed nose gear and right engine/propeller damage.Numerous maneuvers had been performed involving several landing gear extension retraction cycles; and 5 takeoffs and landings; all normal until last 3 patterns during which nose gear initially showed locked then unsafe. Several touch and go landings(3) were performed during which we attempted to lightly touch nose wheel to move into locked position and get the safe indication. Some of those attempts were firm enough to confirm gear was actually down and locked. Landing gear hydraulic lever had returned to center and gear was visible in mirror every time. Checklist items for a single light out; handle returning to neutral; gear warning horn active was followed and in addition three touchdown taps indicated to me gear was extended. Discussed with student all actions and elected to land on Runway XY instead of active [Runway] XX so we could land; roll out gently; stop; and shut down so I could visually inspect the gear. After we were cleared to land on Runway XY I feathered left engine on base; continued approach; conducted gump's and final checks. As main gear contacted runaway I pulled mixture on number two engine and although initial touchdown was normal; aircraft began a slight yaw to the right along with some unusual noise like rubbing or scuffing. Felt similar to right main tire going flat quickly followed by greatly increasing yaw; much worse than a flat tire. We applied left full rudder pedal but yaw was increasing dramatically aircraft was nearly 30 degrees to centerline and about to leave runway. As there are no wheel brakes on my side of aircraft so I loudly instructed student 'left break; left break; left brake; left brake 'which he did; straightening out aircraft parallel to centerline approximately 6 ft. from edge of runway. Shortly after this nose gear collapsed and remaining 1 to 200 ft. of runway was done on the nose of the aircraft and the main gear. Once stopped; we shut off master; generators; avionics; fuel and vacated aircraft. Myers aviation removed airplane and put in our hanger. Upon inspection and disassembly it was discovered that nose wheel was turned past the stops to the right; tire scuff marks; and hydraulic actuator bent 90deg in fully extended position most likely due to excessive side load. Upper drag link assembly tubing cracked; separated; other parts bent or damaged and all located except one turn limit stop pin.

Aircraft Y in front of me was given the instruction first and immediately started their turn to the right. When I was given the instruction; I waited to try to ask Gateway Tower what they meant; but the frequency was too busy. I decided to start the turn to the right to make a 360 to re-enter the downwind. Unfortunately; my slow thinking led to me making a turn at the same time that the aircraft in front of me was already almost finished with their turn. This resulted in a near head-on collision. The other aircraft fortunately realized this; pulled up and turned to their right promptly. I saw the aircraft fly over me and assumed it was an aircraft coming south from the gap with an odd pattern entry. Although a bit flustered; I was able to land the airplane and thought of it as a bad coincidence. The flight instructor on-board the other aircraft in the incident; approached me after my flight and asked to discuss once I returned. We discussed the incident and my flight instructor who was not on-board my solo flight; was also notified and joined us in the debrief.

column121: When I was assigned a Tower position I inquired as to working a different position as it was my 6th day working and my last round of the day. I was told no. When I got to the tower it appeared to me that Local Control and Ground Control had been on position for the same amount of time. I went to relieve Ground Control and the Supervisor told me 'no your not going to ground' when I inquired about the the time on position he told me that Local Control had been on position over 2 hours. I again asked if I could work Ground Control. The Supervisor did not answer and ordered me to go to Local Control.Another controller in the tower said the Local Controller had requested to go from a previous position to Local when he was relieved without a break. When I first assumed the position the Supervisor asked me if I wanted him to write some of the call signs on the strips. I declined since it did was not busy at the time. This session turned into a heavy arrival push with some departures and multiple crossings. There were numerous data tags constantly overlapping as well as approximately one half separation between several arrivals making it difficult not only to write down the aircraft call signs on the half strips used for this position but also to ensure the preceding arrival was off the runway prior to the succeeding aircraft crossing the landing threshold.The Supervisor stood at the Cab Coordinator position (which was not staffed) actively listening the entire time I was on position. The only coordination performed by the Supervisor was to tell me I could issue a 110 heading out of 1;500 feet which at the time was completely unnecessary as well as a distraction. Aircraft X had been cleared to land and hold short of taxiway whiskey for crossing traffic. I had an Aircraft Z that was going to do a missed approach with a 030 heading behind Aircraft X. Aircraft Y had previously called ready for departure I cleared Aircraft Y for departure then realizing it was not going to work when I did my 3 part scan I complete prior to every departure. I immediately went back to Aircraft Y and cancelled takeoff clearance and instructed them to hold short. The aircraft did not acknowledge; and even if a readback was accomplished and complied with; crossing the hold short line was inevitable. I chose to transmit to Aircraft X to get off the runway to prevent a possible departure creating a more dangerous situation. I have not had the opportunity to listen to the tape but I am almost positive Aircraft X exited the runway at an intersection. Aircraft Y was still northbound entering the runway when Aircraft X exited the runway. Aircraft Y was on the runway on an easterly heading and asked to verify if cleared for departure. I advised negative and instructed to hold in position to alleviate any further confusion on Aircraft Y part. After a short time went by I then cleared Aircraft Y for departure. At that point the Supervisor asked me if there was anything he needed to be looking into.I advised since he wasn't aware of what happened 'I didn't know' and then told him what is written above. I think it would be a good idea if a new Supervisor who may not be fully aware of the ins and outs of the facility during extreme pushes to have a Cab Coordinator opened. Also for whatever the reason; the Supervisor is unable to keep abreast of what is happening while actively listening with a headset standing 3 feet from the busiest position; then opening a Cab Coordinator would have been a good call. Perhaps a Cab Coordinator would have caught the situation not going to work prior to my clearing the aircraft for departure to begin with and would have definitely helped with the numerous crossings.

column121: I was conducting a training flight and was headed to N40. Approximately 4 miles south of the airport; I made a radio call on UNICOM announcing I was 4 miles south at 2;000 feet descending to pattern with intentions to join the left downwind Runway 25 using a standard 45 degree entry. As I continued to approach the airport; I was scanning in front; to the left; and to the right of me while listening to the radio for relevant traffic. When I was about to make my entry to join a left downwind; I made a radio call announcing that I was joining the downwind leg of Runway 25. Prior to turning; I made a quick scan to the left; center; and right. I did not see any traffic. As I started my turn; I scanned left again and saw a Piper on downwind approximately 200 feet horizontally to the left of my aircraft and 60 feet vertically beneath me. Simultaneously; I heard the Piper make a radio call announcing they were breaking off the downwind and saw the Piper turn away from my aircraft. I judged that the situation was under control so I continued my turn to join downwind and made a radio call to the Piper stating that I had him in sight and apologized for cutting him off in the pattern. The rest of the flight was uneventful. Contributing factors include: 1; Either a lack of an initial radio call from the Piper; or myself missing the radio call from the Piper. 2; I had made a radio call that I was making a 45 degree entry to join the left downwind; but mispositioned my aircraft and made a turn closer to 90 degrees instead. This positioning error may have led the Piper to scan the wrong area. 3; Too fast a scan to detect an aircraft against the backdrop of the ground 4; Busy UNICOM frequency with a lot of radio calls from multiple airports. Regarding human performance considerations; I made a poor judgment to continue to approach the airport directly from the south rather than change course to put the aircraft into a better position for a 45 degree entry to downwind. Additionally; as I was not aware of any radio calls for an aircraft in the pattern at N40; I should have conducted a more thorough scan to look for unexpected aircraft. While I was scanning in all directions; I moved from one sector to another relatively quickly which likely caused me to miss the Piper and reinforce my perception that there were no other aircraft in the pattern. To prevent a recurrence of the situation; I will start thinking about my initial approach direction to an airport further out than I currently do. This should help ensure proper positioning for entry into the pattern and help other traffic locate me. I will also improve my scan and spend more time on each sector. This should greatly improve my ability to spot any unexpected aircraft.

column121: I was a CFI giving instruction to a first-time tailwheel student in a Aircraft X. The Aircraft X [vintage aircraft] primary trainer that lacks an electrical system and therefore has no radios with which to communicate with other aircraft. The only electronic equipment onboard is a 406 ELT and a battery powered intercom to allow communication between instructor and student. We had finished the airwork/aircraft familiarization portion of our flight and had returned to the traffic pattern for takeoff and landing practice. We operate out of ZZZ; [local city]; just north of downtown. ZZZ is a busy GA airport with heavy flight school traffic; helicopter traffic; and [vintage aircraft] traffic in the form of [vintage military]; aerobatic; and vintage aircraft. The local flight school is well aware of our [aircraft type] operation and it always extra vigilant of possible NORDO traffic because we operate regularly. Worth noting is that Runway XX [north] utilizes a left-traffic pattern while Runway XX [south] uses right-traffic. This is due to obstacles east of the airport and to keep all traffic over the river rather than over the city. The weather at the time of the incident was good VFR; nearly unlimited visibility with northeast wind of 5-10 kts. The windsock unmistakably favored Runway XX [north] all day and was consistent. I had been at the airport since late morning and everyone had been using Runway XX [north] all day. When in the pattern and scanning for traffic; I noted that we were the only aircraft in the area; but a flight school aircraft was taxiing out for departure on Runway XX [north]. On approach to our first landing; I noticed the Aircraft Y holding short and appeared to be waiting for us to land. After we crossed the threshold; the Cessna taxied into position to depart. After our touch and go and on the upwind leg; my student exclaimed 'dude what's that?' I leaned around him (I was in the rear seat) to see an airplane filling our windshield. I quickly took control and aggressively turned into the downwind. While in the turn; I observed an Aircraft Z pass behind us on final to Runway XX [south]. I estimate the horizontal separation to be 1000 feet or less and vertical separation to be less than 50 feet. Once in the downwind; I observed the Aircraft Z that had taxied into position behind us execute an emergency turn off the Runway; presumably as surprised as I was to see an airplane landing on the opposing Runway with a very obvious tailwind.From the downwind; I witnessed Aircraft Z land and clear the Runway. The Cessna was still holding short; so I executed a short approach and put the Aircraft X on the ground as quickly as possible; student and self very shaken. I taxied to parking in front of the hangar and shut down. I noticed the Aircraft Z pilot was walking toward us; presumably to apologize. Instead; he verbally accused my student and me of causing a dangerous situation by not having a radio. I reminded him of the windsock and weather conditions which clearly favor Runway XX [north] to which he replied that he got his weather report from 'Center' and they told him winds were calm. He then informed me that he made several radio calls; including 'left downwind; left base; and final for XX [south]'. I reminded him that Runway XX [south] utilizes a right traffic pattern; so nobody would be looking for him on the east side of the airport. After a short discussion with the instructor in the aircraft involved; he never heard any radio calls from the offending Aircraft Z other than his last call that he was clearing Runway XX [south]. His account of the entire incident was identical to mine; as we discussed it with the event still very fresh in our minds. He has offered to provide a written statement as well.I am 100% confident that we did nothing wrong nor did we violate any FAR's. I am submitting this report purely for the need for such a close call to be documented and hopefully learned from in the future. The negligence of an irresponsible pilot nearly caused a mid-air collision; and did cause a Runway incursion. If it were up to me; some serious remedial training would be required for the offending pilot to continue to use his privileges as a pilot. Everyone makes mistakes or misses a 'RP' [right-hand pattern] note on a sectional chart from time to time; but when that minor error almost gets people killed; something should be done. His defensive and rude 'I didn't do anything wrong; its your fault for not hearing me' attitude certainly didn't indicate to me that he realized the seriousness of his actions. I sincerely hope this report can be of use to others in the future and a harsh reminder to us all of the unforgiving nature of flying at an uncontrolled field.

I noticed I was a bit high at 900 feet when I turned over the shopping center so 100 feet above where I normally am. Put in some more flaps to about 20 degrees and turned in to final. I saw 3 whites and 1 red light; so I knew I was a bit high; I reduced power to get the plane to slow and reduce elevation. This gets me to the railroad tracks and descending in normally. Power is reduced to idle over the railroad tracks near Runway XX airplane starts to decent quicker than the last 2 times that I landed solo. As a result; I pitched up to get the glare shield on the horizon as that happened; I touched down and bounced on the runway. As the aircraft rose; I pitched for a decent angle thinking I was high above the runway; as the nose came over; I was surprised how close to the runway I was. Then I pitched for level flight; as I did this the aircraft touched down for a second; I thought It touched flat. But the nose dropped even more; this is when I heard the prop strike the runway. The aircraft went out of control veering to the left; as it departed the runway the nose gear collapses and digs into the dirt. The forward momentum of the airplane has the tail lifted off the ground before aggressively landing on the mains. the aircraft has come to a full stop; after stopping I paused for 3 seconds and then I contacted Tower and let them know what happened. After contacting Tower; I Opened my door and took off the seat belt; took the headset off and stepped out of the plan. I went out of the aircraft for 30 seconds before going back and turning the ignition off and turning off the master switch. After that I was met by airport ops.  After the initial shock and recuperating my thoughts I have found what mistakes I made on this solo and how this should have been avoided. Firstly; there is the initial bounce and when I caught air; I should have pushed into full power and pitched up to have the glare shield on the horizon which allows me to climb and then radio into Tower for a go-around. Definitely do not pitch down like I did and try to save the landing but rather go full power and pitch up for a climb. I was very appreciative of the airport ops and their quick action to make sure that I was safe and getting all the information to see how I didn't land correctly.

column121: I had just crossed the threshold for landing on Runway 18 when ATC announced 'Aircraft X on short final; go-around.' I had been cleared for landing as number three; with additional aircraft behind me; and had been directed to follow the Aircraft Y in front of me.
