I landed while the airplane in front of me was still on the runway; about 500-600 feet ahead. I heard ATC's direction; but assumed that it was for the airplane behind me and was concerned that climbing back in the pattern would put me in front of the other airplane that was going around. After landing; ATC gave me a phone number to call them and I did; explaining to them my perspective of the situation. As a student pilot; I had been told not to land when another airplane was on the runway; but failed to recall that during the landing because the round out was in progress and requiring my full attention. The experience of having to call the Tower and be reminded that I cannot land when another airplane is on the runway; irrespective of how far ahead that airplane may be; has burned the lesson into memory; and while I may make other errors; I will not repeat this one.

column121: Upon landing on runway XX; we bounced slightly and then got hit by a gust from the left. As we re-contacted the ground; we were in a rightward drift and the learner failed to input a sufficient crosswind correction and I failed to call for a go-around. We slewed to the left into a ground loop causing minor scraping to the right wing tip.We taxied to the ramp and shut down and got out to inspect the airplane; finding minor skin damage to the right wing tip outboard of the aileron. We then decided to terminate the lesson.The learner (and airplane owner) had been off of flying for several weeks and had engaged me to help him get current again. We pre-briefed our plan of action and reviewed the weather and traffic conditions during an hour of ground school prior to starting up. The weather was good VFR with winds 270/9. I briefed that the forecast included a chance of winds gusting to 17 knots and that ZZZ might be busy on a nice Sunday afternoon. We took off and climbed up to 4;000' MSL and practiced some air work including engine failure turn back drills. We then entered the pattern at ZZZ Airport; to begin the pattern work. I was surprised that the pattern did not seem to be busy with only one other airplane in the pattern.  Everything had gone quite well until the gust caught us and I confess that I had begun to relax a bit too much and failed to call a go around after the bounce. As we finished up; I noted that the wind had shifted to 230/12G19; definitely over our stated max for the lesson. In retrospect; I should have been more assertive about not using the paved runway for the first few landings but should have suggested moving on to another airport with a good grass strip aligned with the wind. I should also have remained fully alert to the possibility of a poor first landing attempt.

After going missed from a circling approach to runway XX at ZZZ; the instructor simulated an engine failure by reducing the left throttle to idle. I went through the memory items for the engine failure after takeoff as I had practiced them in the simulator. With the single engine I climbed to 2000 feet and was vectored onto the ILS XX approach. Approaching minimums; my instructor told me to remove the view limiting device and I saw the runway. Shortly thereafter; he told me to go missed. I performed the missed approach flow but when I advanced the throttles; the airplane drifted to the left of the runway and did not climb. I had retracted the gear and flaps according to the procedure; but when we realized we were going to make contact with the ground; my instructor extended the landing gear. column123: During my third training flight in the light twin aircraft; we performed the LOC XX approach into ZZZ; concluding with a circle to runway XX1. We went missed from runway XX1 and flew straight out. During the climb; the instructor simulated an engine failure by retarding the left throttle to idle. I performed all the memory items as I had practiced them in the simulator: while maintaining directional control and airspeed; I smoothly moved the mixtures; then props; then throttles to the full forward position; and then when I had determined that the left engine was the failed one; I placed the left fuel pump forward to the high position. The left throttle was at idle. Then I reached for the left engine mixture control. I expected my instructor's hand to be blocking the quadrant but it wasn't. I checked with him and he told me to continue with the procedure. I reduced the left mixture to idle after which he pushed the control forward slightly. I reduced the left prop to feather and then he pushed this forward slightly as well. After the memory items; I pulled out the QRH to complete the procedure. During this time ZZZ tower switched us over to approach and we requested the ILS XX. My instructor was on the radios. When I opened the QRH; he told me to turn the autopilot on; which I did. After that; I completed the engine failure flow according to the QRH; except that I only touched and verbalized the items relating to the left engine; and did not move any switches. We were vectored for the ILS XX approach and I ran the in-range and before landing checklists according to the QRH. On final approach; my instructor had brought the left engine mixtures and props full forward. Just before minimums; he told me to look up and I saw the runway in front of me. The PAPIs indicated that I was on glidepath and we were set up for a landing in the touchdown zone. He told me to go around. I pressed the mixture controls forward (they were already full forward); then the propeller controls (already full forward); then throttles full forward; and began to apply back pressure and as I did so. I noticed the airplane did not respond as it had during the previous go-around. The airplane was drifting to the left of the runway center line. I retracted the flaps. Then I retracted the landing gear. All of this happened within a matter of seconds. The airplane was significantly left of center line; flying over the grass. I tried to use the aileron and rudders to fly a straight course. It was not climbing at the rate I expected. I scanned the controls and instruments to see what could be the matter. Everything seemed to be in place. I noticed the airspeed was low-- around 80 knots-- and I released back pressure to prevent a stall. At this point I realized that my instructor was speaking loudly and with urgency about the landing gear. I had just retracted the landing gear. Thinking that he wanted to reduce drag for the climb; I told him 'landing gear is retracted.' He reached across the cockpit and placed the gear in the down position. It was at this point that I realized that he wanted the gear down because we were going to make contact with the ground. Within seconds of him placing the gear in the down position; we did make contact with the ground. I believe he and I both were at the controls at this point. We contacted the ground hard once; bounced slightly; then contacted the ground again; at which point the airplane veered to the left and came to a stop.My instructor contacted tower and told them that there were no injuries. Tower said emergency vehicles were on their way. I motioned to the switches and asked 'should we turn them off?' He said 'yes-- battery and alternators [motioning with his hand] and magnetos.' I turned these off; then the pump switches. I then looked out the window and surveyed the damage. I saw the tip of the left wing in contact with the ground; the bent props of the left engine; and the long groove in the turf created by thedragging left wheel. Then emergency personnel arrived and we exited the airplane.I saw the left fuel pump on high after the airplane came to a stop. I think the fuel pump being left on high flooded the engine; preventing it from supplying power during the go-around. Prior to this flight I had done a couple of simulator sessions involving an engine failure; and I had witnessed several simulator sessions which involved engine failures. During all of these sessions; the fuel pump on the faulty or inoperative engine was brought to high. During one simulator session; the instructor made a point of showing that this could solve the issue.I do not remember being told that during an actual training flight in the airplane; the pump should not be turned to high. During the previous training flight; I was told that on the inoperative engine I should only 'touch and tell' and not flip switches. I remembered this and did not flip any switches dealing with the left engine during my flight; which meant that I kept the left fuel pump on high.1. Make it more clear in training that the fuel pump being turned to high can cause the engine to flood and fail to restart. 2. Before doing a simulated engine failure in flight; make it more clear that the fuel pump being turned to high is the one memory item that ought to be simulated... or; that instead of 'touch and tell' on all the items related to the failed engine; it should be 'touch and tell on all items except the fuel pump; which should be turned to the off position'

At this time with the aircraft at a complete stop; I called on CTAF for ZZZ to let other aircraft know we were disabled on the runway; unable to taxi due to the left main tire being flat. At this time we left power to the aircraft to allow usage of the radios to monitor while my rear seated passenger (a student observing our lesson) made a call to the local FBO to request a tow. The workers at the FBO NOTAM'ed the runway closed for 1 hour to allow safe removal of the aircraft from the runway environment. column121: I was acting as a flight instructor on board Aircraft X; a Cessna 172S on a local IFR flight practicing approaches. My student is a Certified Flight Instructor (CFI) candidate who was gaining instrument currency and proficiency. We began with an ILS approach at ZZZ1 with my student flying the aircraft and me handling ATC communications to reduce his workload in the hard IMC conditions. We crossed a cold front while receiving vectors for the ILS approach where we encountered light to moderate turbulence and precipitation. We completed the ILS approach without incident and proceeded to the VOR for the VOR-A approach into ZZZ; planning to complete a Low Approach Only. We experienced severe turbulence which forced the autopilot (GFC700) to disconnect and I took the controls of the aircraft and requested deviations to the north as necessary to track clear of the progressing cold front. Once we got into smoother air; I gave my student the flight controls and we proceeded direct ZZZ2 [VOR] for a procedure turn. Our plan was to complete the VOR-A approach and then receive radar vectors for the RNAV 01 at ZZZ. My student had proclaimed that he wanted to avoid going back through the cold front while getting vectored for the RNAV 01 approach and suggested we circle to land at ZZZ and cancel the IFR flight plan. When my student suggested this; we had passed the Final Approach Fix inbound and began a descent to the Minimum Descent Altitude and were switched over to advisory frequency. I switched frequencies back to Approach to tell them our intentions to try and circle to land since they were expecting us to go missed on the practice approach. When I told ATC of our intentions; they replied in the affirmative and added 'Aircraft X; low altitude alert; check altitude immediately; altitude indicates 1;800.' I replied the altitude checks and requested an altimeter setting. ATC replied with an altimeter setting of 29.58 and we had a setting of 29.67 set in. I figured this was why they gave us the low altitude alert but then quickly realized that the Minimum Descent Altitude for the segment of the approach we were on was 2;020 feet and we were at 1;720 feet with the new altimeter setting. I informed my student to return to 2;020 feet and we continued on the approach without issue and proceeded with the missed approach with vectors to the RNAV01 at ZZZ. During the missed approach; I was surprised at myself that I did not catch that the student had descended below the Minimum Descent Altitude and I assessed why that had happened during a period of smooth flight and during the post flight discussion with my student. During the lead up to the approach; the encounter with the severe turbulence had shaken both me and my student. We also had a back seat passenger who was an instrument student who had never been in IMC before. I was concerned with the safety of my student and the back seat student and began thinking about the circle to land approach and how we would request vectors for the RNAV Approach if we were unable to circle to land in order to stay away from the front line. I had determined from the weather when we departed ZZZ that circling for the runway at ZZZ would have been nearly impossible with the current ceilings. I told my student this and informed him we would need to execute the RNAV Approach in order to make it back into the airport.The workload at the moment was very high and the effects of the turbulence certainly could have impaired multitasking skills for both my student and I. When we began the descent on the approach; we left 3;000 feet for 2;020 feet which is the Minimum Descent Altitude until a fix which then the Minimum Descent Altitude decreases to 1;760 feet. My student did not reset the altitude select when we ran our Final Approach Fix check and the altitude select remained at 3;000 feet. Additionally; when I recognized we were below the published Minimum Descent Altitude; I should have instructed my student to execute the missed approach as 91.175(E)(1)(i) states; rather than just climbing back up to the Minimum Descent Altitude.This flight was also my third flight in hard IMC this day; and this VOR approach was my 8th approach in IMC in a span of 6 hours. I am an experienced Flight Instructor with over 45 hours in actual instrument conditions and over 150 approach logged; but never before had I completed so many IMC flights in such a time span with the challenging conditions of the frontal passage. My self-assessment prior to this flight determined I was able to complete the flight successfully with good quality of instruction to the student; but the extraordinary conditions we experienced during the flight quickly eroded that ability for me; in addition to the highly divided workload situation we found ourselves in while inbound on the VOR Approach which led to the descent below Minimum Descent Altitude and failure to execute the missed approach immediately after. I think also a more comprehensive briefing of the approach would have aided in my student's short term memory of the initial difference of Minimum Descent Altitude. Even though I briefed the Minimum Descent Altitudes; I do not think they were retained due to the stress and workload of the situation. If this event were to occur again; I would better instruct my student to execute the missed approach rather than working to reclaim the missed Minimum Descent Altitude.
column123: The aircraft had 3 people on board for a local approaches flight in IMC conditions in Aircraft. This flight took place while a stationary front was passing through the area. This caused for almost constant moderate turbulence at times during the flight close to the frontal passage. The flight started with an ILS approach into ZZZ1. After the ILS approach we were vectored to go to the ZZZ2 VOR . Along the way; we had to deviate twice for turbulence. This; as well as IMC conditions; was causing a good amount of sensory overload for myself and the flight instructor with me. At times during the flight the autopilot was being used; but at one point; the amount of turbulence actually caused the autopilot to disengage. Because of this; at the time of the deviation; I was hand flying the aircraft while the other pilot was loading the VOR Approach. When we proceeded inbound on the approach; there is a step down to a minimum of 2;020 feet until an 8 DME fix. Then the minimum goes lower to 1;760 feet. With the sensory overload that both I and the other pilot were experiencing during the IMC flight; we ended up descending below the altitude minimum below the fix. ATC had not updated our altimeter setting in a decent amount of time. We were called by ATC letting us know for a low altitude and to immediately recover. They gave us an updated altimeter and our altitude after the correction showed it being right at the approach total minimum. Instead of executing an immediate missed approach we climbed back up to 2020 feet then re-descended to the 1;760 minimums. By doing this we unfortunately broke 14 CFR 91.175 (c) 1; 3 and (e) 1. The proper action would have been to either; not conduct the flight in the first place or; to immediately execute the missed approach once realizing the descent below the step down. We also could have stopped the flight after the ILS approach into ZZZ1. The rest of the flight utilized great CRM; but during this approach; a better action to even ask as the approach started would have been to double check the approach and its minimums including each step down.

column121: I was providing instruction to my instrument student.  He was in the left seat; flying the plane on autopilot; having been cleared by me (simulating ATC) to proceed via direct to the ZZZ VORTAC at 9;500 MSL; there to commence the RNAV XX approach; expecting a circle-to-land.  I obtained approval from the ZZZ tower for this practice approach; with the usual caveats about maintaining VFR; no traffic separation provided; etc.  That approval was granted while we were still about 10 miles west of the VORTAC; inbound to it at 9;500 MSL and perhaps 130 mph indicated. The top of ZZZ Class D is XX00 MSL; and we had no need to enter the Class D until we were final approach fix inbound.Soon after getting approval from the tower for the practice approach; the tower informed us that there was traffic at about our 10 o'clock; southeast bound.  I saw it immediately both visually and on our GPS nav screen.  It appeared to be a white high-wing LSA (Light Sport Aircraft); either a Remos or a Flight Design.  I can't recall if the tower was talking to that plane; but I'd guess not; as the traffic advisory was issued only to our own tail number; as I recall.I watched the LSA carefully as my student (via our A/P (Autopilot); in NAV mode) took us towards the VORTAC.  We seemed to be converging slowly; with only a 20 or 30 degree difference in our headings; and exactly the same altitude.  The LSA was rock-steady in maintaining its heading and altitude; and seemed to be on A/P; also heading for the local VORTAC.We were slowly closing on the LSA; holding a constant bearing about 30 or 40 degrees behind its right wing.  As the distance between us decreased to about a mile; I instructed my student to make a serious power reduction; which he would have done anyway over the VORTAC.  I thought that this would change the equation enough that we would fall behind the LSA.  After half a minute (or less); I realized that we were not slowing enough to make an appreciable difference in our closure; so I told my student to put his heading bug about 45 degrees off to the left of our heading; and punch the HEADING button on the A/P; which he did.  Our 185 then made a nice standard-rate turn to the left; and we passed directly behind the LSA; exactly at its altitude and about 500 feet away.  The LSA never wavered - as if he never saw us.After about a minute on our new heading; I 'cleared' my student from present position direct to the VORTAC to commence the approach.  We heard nothing from the LSA; nor did we see it again.  The practice approach and landing were without incident.As I recall; we were always behind the wing of the LSA; so we were the overtaking aircraft.  I fault myself for waiting too long before starting the turn to break the slow-motion convergence with the other airplane.  There was no chance that we were going to collide with it - I never stopped watching it; and I am an experienced formation pilot; good at judging closure rates and angles; etc. But I did not allow for the possibility that the LSA might make a sudden sharp turn towards us; or that its pilot might look out to his right rear and be unpleasantly surprised to see us there. If such a situation were to arise again; I would make an earlier turn or altitude change to get a good resolution; and try to keep a mile away from the converging traffic.  It makes more sense; doesn't cost any more; and sets a better example for my student pilot.

I then radioed the tower at ZZZ1 on their frequency and identified myself as a student pilot solo flight along with my relative position west of the airport and requested a full-stop landing while approximately 15nm away.The Tower answered saying they were having difficulty hearing my transmission and to restate my position. I spoke more loudly and clearly; identifying my position as west at about 14.6 miles. They advised me to re-contact them when less than a mile from the runway.  I began a descent appropriate to arrive at pattern altitude prior to radio contact. When I got within a mile I radioed the tower and the tower advised me to turn for my base and that I was cleared to land. I executed turns to base and final without issue and extended full flaps incrementally. Upon entering final approach with full-flaps I was just high of the glideslope as indicated by the PAPI system. I entered my flair and 'ballooned' slightly. When I came back down from ballooning; I came down hard and in the process; experienced prop strike; front gear collapse; and damage to my right wing before coming to a stop on the grass to the left of the runway with the help of the grass to arrest my momentum. The plane came to rest in a nose-down fashion at an approximate 45 degree angle to the edge of the runway and in the direction of the landing. After announcing over the radio that they have a crash on the runway; the tower radioed me to ask my condition and I replied that I was fine. I then noticed fuel leaking from my right wing and elected to shut down electrical items as a precaution. When the airport firetruck arrived; the operator sprayed foam on the area leaking as a precaution for the fuel leak. After several minutes; the responding airport staff strapped the nose wheel to the fuselage and were able to pull the plane to a storage hangar with a tractor by keeping the plane on the main landing gear and tugging the plane via the tail tie-down.

column121: My student and I departed on a training flight to the southeast practice area where we were going to run through Private Pilot maneuvers (stalls; steep turns; engine out; ground maneuvers and landings). After climbing to 035 and completing steep turns; we set up to do power on stalls and climbed to 050. We then set up to do power off stalls. After completing 4 power off stalls; we still had significant altitude and I decided to give student an engine out by pulling the mixture. The student set up the aircraft for best glide and selected an airfield that was about three miles away and ran through the restart checklist. Every 1500 feet I would advance the mixture and push forward on the yoke to make sure the engine was staying primed. We then simulated part of the forced landing checklist (ELT; squawk codes; emergency calls) and performed the landing brief.The student chose to try to get to the airfield by going down the downwind then realized that student was too low and close to the runway to safely make it to the field. I asked student what the backup plan was and student selected a field to right of the aircraft that student could easily turn into. Student turned the aircraft to the field and I estimated that student could easily make the landing and that student had the engine back and to do a go-around. I advanced the mixture and the engine sputtered and died and the prop stopped. The student announced that I had the controls and I pointed the airplane to the field that student had selected. I checked the mixture in; shut off valve on; then attempted to restart the engine with the key. After two attempts; I determined that we were too low and shut off the fuel valve and pulled the mixture and landed the plane in the field.There was no damage to the plane; no injuries to myself or my student; and no property damage. Fuel levels were still visible and greater than half way from the top of the tanks (well over 1/2 full; I didn't have a fuel stick to check total actual levels); oil level was still at 5 qts. We were able to later restart the airplane and taxi it closer to the property owner's barn with permission.The biggest thing that I learned was that I will not pull the mixture to simulate an engine out any more. That was the mistake that I feel caused this. In the future; all engine outs will be initiated by pulling the throttle. Though this has been common in my training from private to commercial; it put us in a dangerous situation that I could have avoided.
column123: At the altitude of 4;000 feet my Instructor pulled the mixture in the aircraft to simulate an emergency landing. At that moment I trimmed the plane all the way; pulled the carb heat and pitched the airplane for 60 kts. Next I looked for a place we could simulate the landing and we were just 2-4 miles from [an] airport. We were descending approximately 500 feet per minute. The closer we got I realized that I was too low to make the obstacles. I made the error of not looking at the altitude of the field. Therefore; I looked to my right and there was a large field and I pointed to my instructor that at that moment the safest decision was to do the field on the right. My instructor said that was a good decision and I started my turn to the field.My airspeed was 60; my right hand was on the throttle; which at the time it was all in. My left hand on the controls and my feet on the rudder. A few seconds later my Instructor looked at me and said 'you would have made it' and he decided to end the simulation by putting the mixture all in. However; the engine would not work and my instructor said 'my controls' I restated 'your controls' and he took charge of the plane. He tried turning the engine on a couple times and the propeller would just not move at all. It happened in a matter of seconds. Since I had already lined up the airplane to the field; my Instructor worked hard to fly the airplane until it touched the ground where he applied the brakes after he had landed it safely. We turned all the systems off and removed the key from the starter. We opened the doors and got out of the aircraft. We called the flight school and they came to get us and to see the airplane.

column121: I was conducting a training flight on Airman Certification Standards (ACS) maneuvers to prepare a student for the practical test to be taken within 4 days.  Initially; we conducted normal; short field; and soft field takeoffs and landings without incident.  Then; we departed to the practice area and practiced unusual attitude recoveries; steep turns; slow flight; approach stalls; and departure stalls from 3;000 feet MSL.  That complete; I directed the student to return to the home airport.  On downwind entry; we were 500 feet above pattern altitude.  I considered this a good opportunity to give my student a simulated engine failure and have him continue to the runway.  On downwind; we were at an altitude lower than the student felt comfortable.  He stated that he didn't feel we could make it.  However; to demonstrate that the landing could still be made if the conditions (engine out) were real; I took the controls made a short approach (a banked continuous base to final turn) and lined the aircraft up with the runway in a landing attitude. Unfortunately; during the maneuver I became obsessed with monitoring our airspeed for proper glide speed and maneuvering during the turn at the neglect of ensuring the landing gear was extended.  We landed with the gear retracted. The flare (round out) was at normal altitude and attitude. Overall; it was not a bad landing.  The student caught the error prior to me when we heard scraping.  The aircraft slid and eventually slid off the runway to a point between the runway and taxiway.One human performance consideration may have been a factor.  I have been conducting training in both straight gear and retractable gear C-172s switching between the two on the same day.  That was the case on this day.  I had flown 0.7 [hours] practicing landings with one student in a fixed gear 172 in the morning; driven to a different airport; and flew in this student's retractable 172 in the afternoon. My mindset was fixated on making the landing and not on the differences between the two aircraft.

column121: According to my student: While he was doing solo touch/goes at ZZZ; on his second landing; he touched down left of centerline. He continued to the transient parking area and called ZZZ Tower per their instructions.As the instructor; my student called me to inform me he had run off the runway; no damage had occurred; and he had spoken with the tower and FAA. I did not know he was flying by himself that day and had received no notification from him. I asked him to recount what happened to me several times trying to understand what happened. I called the Tower and confirmed that the winds were variable at 3 knots and visibility was very good. Based on his recount; I do not fully understand how he thought going off the runway was his safest option. I have not offered him any training or instruction that would indicate that was good judgment. He has never landed far off centerline with me in the plane and has never demonstrated that he would ever act in such a way. He and I have logged extensive dual hours at ZZZ doing pattern work; and he has never flown in a way that indicated he would act or make a decision in this manner. He had demonstrated consistently with me that he was able to maintain directional control of the airplane both in the air and on the ground. I have informed him that all of his solo endorsements are no longer valid. I was planning to spend an extensive amount of time with him on the ground and in the air addressing what happened yesterday through re-training; but he has decided to discontinue his flight training at this time. As a result of this incident; I have re-clarified to all students that they must inform me of any time they plan to solo and must receive my permission before doing so. It seemed they were also distracted by a King Air 350 that was handed over to tower from ZZZ Approach and setup for a right downwind for Runway XX. Initially tower had told them to enter left downwind; but they were adamant that they wanted right downwind; which I believe both added to the confusion; as well as tied up the tower frequency unnecessarily with their continued back and forth communications. It did not help that the King Air had requested and was then doing a 360 turn for spacing of their own; right on the upwind leg of Runway XX when there were multiple other aircraft in the traffic pattern.It should be noted that while we were on short final; the Aircraft Y involved in this incident had once again turned base too soon; and I noticed that they were less than 0.5nm behind us.  They were so close that they in fact were ordered to go-around by the Tower because we had just touched down and were still rolling out when they crossed the runway threshold behind us.I believe contributing to the incident were: The pilot of Aircraft Y failing to maintain situational awareness resulting in inadequate spacing thus requesting multiple 360 turns; their failure to adequately scan for traffic and maintain a proper rectangular course in the traffic pattern causing them to cross our final approach course at a 45 degree angle; tower controller being task saturated with multiple aircraft in the traffic pattern; and the King Air traffic adding to the confusion by adamantly requesting to enter the right downwind (which conflicted with the other aircraft already in the traffic pattern for Runway XX; which is right traffic.)

column121: I have departed ZZZ airport to the south to practice landings in ZZZ1. On the way back to ZZZ I have contacted ZZZ Tower around 7NM to 8 NM south of the field; the Tower has replied standby so I have tuned to easterly heading so I will not enter the airspace; a few minutes after that the Tower has instructed me to join mid left downwind for Runway XX and to report when established on the downwind; after I have established on the downwind I have notified the Tower. To the best of my knowledge and memory the Tower has replied the following instruction: 'you are number 3 for Runway XX continue'; I have given the Tower read back and then I looked forward to visually scan for the traffic in front of me; I remember clearly that I saw 2 aircraft in the final for Runway XX; the first one was an airplane in the short final and the second one was a helicopter that was also in the final behind him. I remember that I have pointed the 2 aircraft to my students and explained to them that these are the aircraft that are in front of us and we will follow them as we are number 3 in the sequence. After the helicopter was abeam to my position; I continued to fly on the downwind for an extra 30 seconds to 1 minute so I will allow some extra spacing between myself and the helicopter as I'm flying with students on their first ever fly day. As I was told I'm number 3 in sequence and I visually saw the 2 aircraft that are in front of me I have continued the traffic pattern and turn left to the base leg; and then when I was in the appropriate position I have turned final. Between 30 seconds to 1 minute after I was established on the final for XX the Tower has instructed me to 'immediately turn heading 090 and break the approach'; I have immediately took controls from my student and turned to the heading 090 while giving a read back to the Tower. As I have established on the heading 090 I saw that there was a jet aircraft on the final approach behind me; approximately 1;200 feet horizontally and 300 feet vertically in my evaluation. after that I have continued to comply with the Tower instructions and followed a different traffic that was on the downwind to join the final for Runway XX again for a full stop. Before landing when I was on short final I have verified with the Tower that I had clearance to land.I have strong belief in self critic and self evaluation and after this event has occurred I have come up with the following safety measures that can help prevent this situation from reoccurring:1. When you have been instructed to follow traffic while on the downwind; you should always verify with Tower that you can start your turn towards the base leg.2. When you are told that you are number 3 in sequence and you see the 2 aircraft in front of you; that absolutely does not mean that you should stop looking for other traffic in the area; you still need scan for traffic very frequently.3. When flying on the base leg; even in a controlled airport; you should always try to look for more traffic coming on the final; both behind you and in front of you; and make sure that there is no traffic that can jeopardize the approach before actually making the turn to final.4. Do not think that just because you are flying in a controlled airspace under ATC supervision; you are protected. Always actively scan for traffic and verify ATC instructions.I believe that if I had used these safety measures that I have mentioned above this event could have been prevented. I am glad no damage has been done in this event; and I'm committed to learn from this experience and actively seek to improve myself as a pilot and as flight instructor.

The Tower asked for fuel amount and time; and passengers; to which I replied we had 60 gallons and plenty of time; 2 souls.We did a low approach over [Runway] XXR; and the Tower confirmed that the gear was down and locked. They asked if we would prefer to land on the north runway; which was the active runway. I said yes and planned a soft field landing to [Runway] XXL. She tried pushing it in; which caused the ammeter to spike; so we pulled it out and left it out.The Tower asked if I wanted additional resources waiting on the ground. column121: My student was preforming pattern work at ZZZ. Traffic pattern altitude being used was 1;800 feet. Conditions were VFR. My student made his crosswind; downwind; and final calls every time. At the same time a C182 was operating for a skydive operation out of ZZZ. My students downwinds were always flown to provide clearance for the skydivers designated landing zone. Throughout his 7 landings in the C172; a PT-17 Stearman joined the pattern; not making any radio communication calls so the student paid extra attention to focus on where the Stearman was operating. The Stearman continued to fly low patterns at about 1;300 feet; with tight downwinds right over the skydiving drop zone. The Stearman sometimes would not even take off from the runway. They would add power then come to a complete stop at the end of the runway and taxi back. While the student was downwind midfield; the skydive C182 was holding short of the runway and made a CTAF call they were waiting for the Stearman to to depart.When the student turned base about 1/2 mile from the runway; the C182 announced they were departing. The student then turned to final and made his radio calls. Flaps were extended about 25 to 30 degrees and the student was coming in at about 70 to 75 MPH. At about 500 feet and 1/4 mile final; the Stearman came down in front of the students C172 about 400 feet away in a rapidly descending base to final and cut right in front of the student. The student had no choice but to abort the landing and go-around since they descended to a lower altitude in front of him. The made a CTAF call on 122.8; '<tail number> going around; aircraft on runway'. Adding full throttle and waiting for a positive rate of climb the student retracted the flaps. The student's initial thought was to just fly runway heading and perform a go around but because of the lack of communication his instincts told him they would perform a touch and go. He then made a 30 degree turn to the right of the runway then turned left to fly parallel to the runway and watched below for the Stearman as he gained altitude. To no surprise the Stearman was performing a touch and go.If my student had flown runway heading the Stearman more than likely would have ascended from under him. If he was any lower on my glide slope; and due to lack of communication from the high performance Stearman; his high wing aircraft would not have seen anyone above him; and the Stearman biplanes nature would not have seen him below them and they would have collided on the displaced threshold. The student had plenty of fuel and flew to the west of ZZZ and waited for them to land before returning. The way the pilots of the Stearman were flying a high performance aircraft with no radio; contrary to the flow of traffic; and without observing Part 91 right of way rules while conducting their operations poses a significant safety hazard.

column121: With just 0.9 hrs of PIC time YTD; I arrived at my flying club's towered home field; ZZZ; rested and eager to shake off some rust. My first sign of how much rust I had came when I accepted a Ground instruction to RWY XX but taxied to the nearer RWY XY. After completing my runup; Ground advised me to taxi to RWY XX. I thanked Ground for 'that catch' and received a double-click 'you're welcome.' I paused; ensured I was focused and not letting myself feel rushed; and proceeded to RWY XX. I completed four takeoffs and landings; and after reviewing LiveATC recordings I believe that my radio communications were professional and crisp. Ground did request that I confirm one hold-short instruction; and Tower asked that I confirm a 'give way to helicopter' instruction as part of a 'hold short' read back. However; I acknowledged and complied with all instructions promptly; including hold-shorts; midfield reports; extended down winds; go-arounds; no delay etc.; using proper phraseology. A midair near-miss occurred when two Cessna's with 'XXXX' in their call signs began to turn base at the same time -- Aircraft Y from Right Downwind; and I; Aircraft Z; from Left Downwind. I mistook a 'cleared for the option' instruction for Aircraft Y as being intended for me; and radioed my acceptance for a full stop. I believed Tower had cleared me to land. The conflicting traffic had been advised of 'that Cessna on Left Downwind;' from which I further inferred my own landing priority over this newcomer to the pattern. Upon review of the recordings; it is clear to me that Tower attempted to clarify that the landing clearance was for Aircraft Y; and that the call out to my position was purely advisory for Aircraft Y -- and not a reaffirmation of a clearance for Aircraft Z to land. However; someone stepped on the frequency; and I missed the clarification. It was only after Tower instructed me; 'You need to turn right now' that I saw the conflicting traffic approximately 1/2 mile turning right base. Tower then instructed me for the first time that I was #2 for the field. I attribute this near-miss primarily to my own lack of recency; but secondarily to additional factors. I lost situational awareness of other similarly-[call] signed Cessna's entering the pattern from the opposite direction. ATC could have clarified our landing sequence earlier; or verbally emphasized the differences in our call signs. (A minute later; Tower itself briefly confused two call signs; instructing me to turn Right Base when I was already on Short Final from Left Base; Tower quickly corrected itself when I advised of my position.) It was also a very busy pattern in which to shake off rust -- for pilots and ATC alike. Simultaneous radio transmissions obscured instructions that might otherwise have been sufficiently clear. Stress was apparent: After landing; I complied immediately with Tower's instruction to exit without delay -- only to be told urgently to 'stop right now' to avoid a jet on its takeoff roll. (I appreciate Tower's urgency: I had acknowledged the hold-short instruction and was already preparing to stop; but to their eyes I was still in 'no delay' mode as I transitioned from RWY to Taxiway.) Tower similarly expressed frustration with another pilot for requesting 'a turn around a point;' a term that Tower did not recognize; they doubtless would have preferred 'a 360' or 'a circle.' When I was finished with my pattern work; I briefly expressed my appreciation to Tower and received a friendly 'no problem' in response. I think we all did what we could to be as clear as possible (urgently if the situation demanded it); and to correct our mistakes. Although it will be frustrating at times; on balance I think this is a good set of attitudes to have; especially as the entire National Airspace System shakes off varying degrees of rust coming out of the pandemic. The dangers here were addressed; but a slightly more intransigent attitude; or a slightly more congested frequency; might have tipped the balance to a midair collision.

If you rolled over too fast it was possible for the plane to want to become temporarily airborne. There were some very tall trees on final and it was a good idea to touch down as close to the threshold as possible. The idea was to fly a very stabilized approach as low as possible over the trees and then get into the flare just as we were crossing the shore of the lake where the runway began. Set up a long straight-in over Garfield Bay; crossed the shore when I realized I did not recognize the landmarks at the lower altitude we were at; and was already descending to what I thought were the tops of the trees on final. Then my student who knows the area well spotted the landmarks I needed. Set up the steep approach and the rest went better than expected. Contributing factors were [the] challenging approach and landing in the type of plane we were flying had me anxious- would have been really easy in a Aircraft X. More challenging to me than landing at Telluride with a 25 gusting 35 crosswind during light snow (Aircraft Y). I did not pick out my landmarks for the approach with the idea I could not orient so well when down low. Did not do a low approach to check out the runway where I wouldn't be so worried about getting stabilized on the approach early- we just overflew the airport at pattern altitude having taken off from Timber Basin about 40 minutes earlier. Did not just do a left downwind/base/final because I was worried about being super-stabilized for the short/soft field landing.  I could have just done a longer downwind and my orientation would have been very good. The high terrain on the left downwind had something to do with my decision. How to avoid [is to] do a better job of picking out landmarks for making an approach plan to challenging airports. Fly the pattern as long as it is safe. At short unprepared strips with tall trees all around it do a low approach and check things out; ensure safety and make a good plan.

column121: While piloting my aircraft at Northern Colorado Regional Airport (FNL); I was holding short of Runway 33 at Taxiway A1; and I contacted the Tower and requested to takeoff Runway 33 and remain in the pattern for landing Runway 33.  Tower cleared me for takeoff; advising me of an aircraft just departing ahead on Runway 33.  I was instructed by the Tower to remain in left closed traffic for Runway 33.After climbing to pattern altitude; I turned crosswind; and then downwind for Runway 33.  While mid-field downwind for Runway 33; I noticed several aircraft targets ahead of me to the south were all converging toward runway 33 on my ADS-B display; one from the east and one from the west; both apparently on base for Runway 33 from opposite directions; and a third target (Aircraft Y) approaching from the southeast.  Spacing among all 3 appeared inadequate.  The Controller told Aircraft Y from the southeast to report 3 mile final.  I was scanning the sky and acquired visual contact on all three aircraft.  Aircraft Y was unable to turn final due to inadequate spacing with the other two aircraft.  I was unable to continue in the standard traffic pattern; as I needed to maneuver east to avoid Aircraft Y as it crossed through final from the southeast and across the downwind to the west; which I estimated to be 500 feet in front of me and 300 feet overhead.  Turning east was the safest alternative to remain clear of Aircraft Y and the other two aircraft; as I had them all in sight. The Controller began shouting to all of the pilots 'I don't have radar!  I see two targets converging to the south!'  The Controller sounded very anxious.  I immediately informed the Tower that I was maneuvering to avoid Aircraft Y now in front and above me.  I recall that the Controller then called one of the other aircraft and said loudly to 'leave the pattern!'; but his instructions were not clear.  He then asked where everyone was located.  I clearly and calmly replied 'Aircraft X; turned left base to avoid the traffic conflict' with Aircraft Y.  The Controller then asked seconds later; 'Who is that on left base?'; and I again replied calmly 'this is Aircraft X on mid-left base.'  He then cleared me to land Runway 33; told the traffic ahead on final to turn east; and then instructed Aircraft Y (now west of the field) to return to land on Runway 33. There was inadequate traffic spacing for incoming traffic entering the pattern; and incomplete awareness by the Controller of the four aircraft positions relative to one another; followed by his distraught demeanor and very exasperated tone as he complained of having no radar feed.  It is also possible that the Controller forgot about my aircraft position in the pattern and that he had instructed me to maintain closed left traffic for Runway 33.  I did my best to remain clear of any traffic conflict; communicate calmly and clearly; and defuse the Controller's anxious situation; while maintaining safe spacing from all traffic in the pattern.  I was cleared to land Runway 33 and did so safely; and taxied to parking as directed by the controller.  No other communication took place between me and the controller.As a recommended solution; the temporary Tower at FNL needs a radar feed installed as soon as possible for better situational awareness for the Controllers.  The Controller's shouting and anxious tone heightened the tension of the situation for the other pilots; which was not helpful in this scenario.  A professional demeanor by the Controller with clear; yet rapid instructions would have been more effective at resolving the traffic conflicts.

column121: Planned flight for the day was to ZZZ1 (for fuel) then to ZZZ. Preflight planning conducted with assistance from ForeFlight mobile application. Departed Runway XX. Climb to 1500 MSL; 14 min cruise to ZZZ1 with landing. Landed at ZZZ1. The flight was conducted satisfactorily. The aircraft was then fueled as necessary.Secondary preflight planning was completed. Satisfactory takeoff and climb out to 7;500 MSL. Approximately 29 minutes; started to notice engine roughness with a significant drop in tachometer RPM. The Pilot in command (PIC) took over as sole manipulator of control and emergency checklist for engine failure in flight initiated. Looked for suitable landing area. Increased in engine RPM occurred and became within glide distance of ZZZ. Engine roughness and drop in RPM began again and ZZZ Tower contacted; advising of need for precautionary landing due to engine roughness. Decision was made to not [get priority handling]. Smooth and satisfactory landing made at ZZZ. After slowing and attempting to turn off Runway; the aircraft did not have any right turning authority. Airplane would only turn left in circle when power applied. Suspected right tire or brake malfunction. Contacted the Tower and asked for permission to shut down aircraft on runway to inspect aircraft.Aircraft was satisfactorily shut down on Runway XY with airport crew arriving for assistance. On post flight walk around; it was found that the right tire became flat; no other external damage grossly observed. Also found to have fluid leak within right pilot side inside firewall. Aircraft was towed to FBO for diagnostics of engine and repair of right tire. When asked if needed to report anything to Tower or FAA; the ZZZ airport crew stated nothing was needed. Furthermore; the Tower did not mention of any need to provide any post flight report during communications. No accident or serious incident occurred.There were a few factors found on post-flight that may have caused the problems:1. Engine Roughness: The engine was new with approximately 28 hours on the engine. Engine during break in period was using Aeroshell 100W. Furthermore; this flight was conducted with cruise altitude at 7;500 MSL. Miscommunication and ill-information about any special procedures regarding aircraft break in were not discussed between aircraft owner and PIC. PIC was told to use 100W oil from previous aircraft owner (box in back of aircraft). Furthermore; the aircraft owner did not provide engine overhaul information or procedures needed for aircraft. On mechanic review; it was found that the left magneto was rotated 17 degrees causing the engine to overheat; an oil line by the firewall was damaged causing a leak; cylinders were glazed; induction air leak; and some crankcase oil leak. Overall a combination of these factors is what probably lead to engine roughness. Post flight testing; the engine performed within specifications 2250 static RPM; 600FPM climb; 2350 dynamic RPM. Engine oil consumption has increased; likely due to glazed cylinders; and is being sent to Company1 for re-honing. Furthermore; the magnetos are being sent in to [Company] Magneto to be re-checked.2. Right Flat Tire: No noted gross evident issues on pre-flight inspection for tires; struts; fairing; or braking systems. Landings was smooth and satisfactory. Theory for tire damage could be due to stuck break after landing and prior to right turn out to taxiway; in conjunction with weak spot on tire and/or a foreign object on runway and/or other. Tire was satisfactorily repaired at ZZZ. Reviewing this scenario there are a few factors to consider. There needs to be improved communication between aircraft owner and operator (PIC); especially during critical times where specific procedures are needed (such as a new engine break in). The right tire flat is a chance occurrence; and I do not think that the flight could have been handled different to prevent. The pilot did all in power to safely shut down the aircraft and immediately check out airplane to prevent any further damage.I have had a clean pilot record; commercial license and CFI. I will use the lessons from this flight for myself and all future students for the purpose of discussing complete airplane maintenance with airplane owners (especially new airplanes); what to do when engine becomes rough; and procedures to follow with a flat tire.

This traffic was flying a significantly wider base than is standard (more than 1/2 to 1 mile from the runway threshold). I initiated an immediate 90 deg left turn; then flew a 270 right turn to enter the final approach.When Tower asks me and other traffic to report a 2 mile right base; I am assuming that I will have a 1/2 to 1 mile final; and that I am just on an extended base leg. I'm wondering if the other pilot flew to a 2 mile final; and then called that as their 2 mile base. I know ZZZ is a Class Delta; but I don't believe they get any supporting radar from ZZZ3. If they were using their eyes to sequence us; then their advisories were unhelpful at best. I don't believe that ZZZ Tower had any accurate idea of where the traffic in the air was at any moment. ZZZ was unaware of how close we came to a collision; and didn't seem to care when I told them I was turning onto a downwind; and then doing a 180 to final. I am the Pilot in Command so [I] take full responsibility for my actions; which were correct in that moment to avoid a collision; but I received no further instructions; which would have been an issue if there had been anybody on a straight-in.In the future; I will be more cognizant of scanning left and right when looking for traffic ahead on a right base. I will be less dependent on Towers with no radar backup to provide me with accurate traffic advisories; or any at all. I believe that Tower Controllers need to be more cognizant of where the traffic is in the air so they can provide better traffic advisories. If they aren't sure where an aircraft is; they should be telling the number 2 airplane to keep a wide scan; rather than acting like everybody is flying a standard pattern.

The airplane was now headed in to the grass safety area after taxiway and I let the plane continue on its track for fear of flipping the plane. This was my second solo flight and the additional load of ATC's inquiry; the follow on instructions to the other plane near my intended runway; and my focus toward the other aircraft may have used more attention than intended. In the FAA 'Airplane Flying Handbook'; after landing roll safety is addressed but does not receive the emphasis it deserves.

The second aircraft from the original flight of two responds traffic in sight and immediately corrects back to the downwind. I respond to 2 other calls then scan back to ensure Aircraft Y was correcting; he wasn't; I say 'Aircraft Y it looks like you are doing exactly what I said not to do; unless the radar is deceiving me here.' Pilot responds 'Aircraft Y was already on base'; I respond 'OK; well I just said don't go on base; you missed that part; so let's go right turn back to the north downwind for both you and the other guy (his flight wing man; who was following instructions)' Pilot responds 'Affirm; right turn; north downwind; Aircraft Y'. I tell the original wing man to now turn base; he correctly responds; I then scan back and see Aircraft Y not following instructions; again the pilot does the opposite and starts a left turn towards final before correcting right and continuing for the north downwind. I then say 'Aircraft Y are you literally on final right now cutting someone off?' Pilot responds 'No; I'm trying to get out of here; we're turning; Aircraft Y'I advise the traffic on final 'Aircraft X; the guy in front of you is moving out of your way; Runway XX cleared to land' His response seemed to be partially blocked but I heard 'Aircraft X'.All aircraft eventually land; brasher warning was not issued. The pilot of Aircraft X called the tower a couple hours later and said he wanted to file a NMAC. He said he was aware of the situation developing and heard the controller (me) several times tell the other aircraft not to turn base and issue instructions which the pilot of Aircraft Y repeatedly disobeyed. I should have issued a traffic alert to both aircraft; but at the minimum to Aircraft X.

column121: The runway incursion occurred when a new CFI and myself were doing a night flight for the said CFI to become night proficient again in small GA aircraft after not flying GA in a long time. ZZZ Tower had closed 30 minutes prior and we were the only aircraft working in the pattern. I said that we should practice a power off 180 when the incursion occurred. The situation that occurred was that Airport Operations was doing sweeps of the runway and either they did not announce they were on the runway or we did not hear them due to being focused on the power off 180 maneuver. As we turn from base to final and get closer to the runway; we did not see anything on the runway that would have warranted a go-around. As we start to line the aircraft up with the runway a few hundred feet above the ground we see on the very edge of the runway two sets of stationary lights that were on the edge that we initially mistook for runway edge lights; but by the time we were about to pass; we saw it was a vehicle. Being low to the ground; still in a bank; low energy; and with nothing in front of us I determined going-around was not the optimal decision to make since the vehicle was now behind us. After seeing it was a vehicle of some sort I initially believed that the sweeper had moved off into the grass; however the driver came over after we landed and said he was still on the runway. We landed 300 ft. past the vehicle to the best of my knowledge so there was no immediate concern for a collision.I believe that the situation would not have occurred had several things happened. A breakdown of communication had occurred in the chain of events between the aircraft and the Ground Operations in terms of knowing the position of where everyone was. We made a downwind call but did not make subsequent calls due to the high workload of the power off 180 maneuver. I cannot confirm if the ground vehicle did or did not make a call; but to the best of my knowledge they did not make the call saying they were on the runway.

At the time I was aware of a TBM aircraft behind and faster then me on an GPS approach for an avionics check; as well as another aircraft 500 ft. below me passing right to left. Tower was extremely busy at the time and I was unable to report the near miss immediately due to frequency volume and traffic. Adding to the confusion there was another aircraft in the area with the abbreviated tail number being Aircraft Y; while my tail number being Aircraft X. Tower told me to turn base which did make sense to me considering I was 5 miles out. I reported to Tower that there were two [similar N-numbers] on frequencies. He then told Aircraft Y to turn base followed by an instruction to me to turn to a heading of 070. I read back 070 but confirmation bias; and still rattled by the near miss; I turned to a heading of 170 thinking that he wanted me to turn an extended base to final; essentially cutting off the faster TBM closing on me. Tower asked me to read off my current heading and I reported flying 175 only then realizing the mistake. I was advised to make a right turn to intercept the final of Runway XX and report turning through 270 degrees. Already heading south this happened in less than 30 seconds. Now inbound on final for landing I was advised to copy a phone number on the ground for a possible pilot deviation. Finally on a half mile final I asked Tower twice if I was cleared to land Runway XX; and they advised me that I was 'still cleared to land XX' when I had not previously been given a landing clearance. Once on the ground I contacted Tower via phone and we discussed the situation; agreeing that parties were at fault a that a lot of events contributed to the situation.I believe that there were 3 main human factors causes that led to this incident.First the Tower was overloaded with inbound; transit; and outbound traffic and was unable to properly give traffic advisories to inbound and departing traffic.Second that Tower instructed me turn base when an aircraft with a similar call sign was the intended recipient even though it didn't make sense to me and at the time. Lastly that because of confirmation bias I expected to receive a base to final clearance when in reality he wanted me to intercept a left downwind entry into the pattern.

Fortunately; I was thoroughly strapped into the four-point restraint harness and was uninjured.In retrospect; I should have abandoned the approach when it became unstable; and initiated a go-around. This will be a very expensive lesson. I am grateful that I emerged from the experience physically unscathed.

column123: I am a Flight Instructor and was practicing landings with my student. We were practicing short field landings and were inbound for the second landing at the airport. On final the student had made the remark we were coming in slightly fast and began correcting for the correct airspeeds. The approach to landing itself was not abnormal.  It was on centerline and at a proper glidepath; just slightly fast. Due to the fact that we had been practicing short field landings; the student was aiming to flare at a point that likely should have been extended. As we flared; a little bit of crosswind caused there to be a slight sideload on the left wheel and at the time it was the only wheel touching the ground. As the Instructor; I had mentioned right rudder to get us realigned with centerline and reduce the sideloading. The student used right rudder but accidentally had his foot on the brake as well as the rudder. This caused the plane to brake solely on the right side and begin skidding down the runway. Out of fear; I believe the brake was pushed slightly more as opposed to less. At this time I started calling that I had the flight controls and the student took his hands off of the controls. At this point; the aircraft was perpendicular to the runway. Momentum had the plane still rolling slowly. I was not sure at the time if there was any damage to the tires due to side load or skidding and did not want to apply brakes in an effort to reduce damage. At this point I treated the plane as if it was a soft field landing; I used minimal braking and let the plane come to a stop in the grass directly next to the runway. I have a very small feet and know for myself that if my heels are on the ground I am on the rudder. In order to touch the brake; my leg needs to be lifted. This is not the case for most other people. In the future; I have now learned that to reduce the chances of this happening again; I will verify on short final that the students have their feet only on the rudder and not touching the brakes. Instead of teaching 'heels on the ground' I will now specify that 'balls of feet should be on the rudders'

To have the FAA breathing down ZZZ's throat for recent mid-airs (both of which were pilot error and had nothing to do with ATC); and then to be directed into a near-collision on base by BJC Tower; is unacceptable; and tells me that the FAA doesn't care until something makes the news.

column121: This occurrence happened after maneuvers. We were practicing normal takeoffs and landings at ZZZ which had a crosswind component of 10 kt. After a first attempt and go-around; we decided to try again. On the second approach in; we proceeded to come in slow; 50 kt.; and I prompted my student to add in power. However; he was frozen and too fixated to notice the low airspeed. I should have promptly issued a go-around and should have taken the controls. However; I was not forceful enough and was not able to take the controls from my student to go around; resulting in a rough landing and a tail strike. We ended up going around and did not feel there was any difference in controls and continued back to ZZZ1.Later after pushing the plane back; we noticed the damaged tail piece and the bent tail strike protection. This could have all been avoided with just a simple go-around. At the slightest feeling of something not going right - for example; not being lined up or being too slow on final - a go-around will ultimately save a bad landing from happening. The student and the instructor should always be communicating and be aware of the situation that is happening. A positive exchange of controls should be practiced frequently so that the exchange can be flawless and can prevent situations where a student may be fixated or task saturated. The reaction to go around was not quick enough and resulted in the tail strike. Task saturation is a real thing; especially if a student pilot is being introduced to a new airport and also uncontrolled airport operations as well. To wrap things up; going around is your best option and positive exchange of controls should be practiced not only when braking; but also while in the air; even in critical phases of flight.
